docs.text: tuvl ¶ Typed workflows of agents — deterministic where they can be, bounded where they can't — on a durable, journaled runtime, built spec-first. tuvl 2.0 tuvl 2.0 is a redesign with no 1.x compatibility layer: workflows are graphs of typed agents , every run is durable and journaled, and projects are built from specs. See what's new . Versions follow SemVer . Try it live — no install Run any example in a throwaway browser sandbox at try.tuvl.online with the Insight editor. Pronounced "Thoo-val" (തൂവൽ) in Malayalam — a feather. What is tuvl? ¶ A tuvl workflow is a graph of agents . Each agent has a typed contract — inputs , outputs , the signals it emits — and an engine that implements it. Signals route to the next agent or a named end. tuvl checks the whole graph statically (contracts, data flow, types, policy, worst-case cost) and runs it on a durable runtime that records everything it does. kind: Workflow version: tuvl/v2 metadata: { name: refund_flow, description: Handle a refund request } spec: models: [Order, Refund] trigger: http: { path: /api/refunds, method: POST } input: { order_id: uuid, reason: str } agents: - id: load_order description: Load the order engine: tool inputs: { order_id: uuid } outputs: { order: Order } tool: { use: db, model: Order, op: read, where: { id: "{{ order_id }}" } } routes: { default: triage, not_found: END.missing, error: END.failed } - id: triage description: Decide how the refund is handled engine: decide inputs: { order: Order, reason: str } outputs: { lane: "enum[auto, review]" } decide: rules: - { when: "order.total > 500", then: review } - { when: "true", then: auto } routes: { auto: issue_refund, review: approval, error: END.failed } # issue_refund (code) and approval (human) … outputs: default: { status: 200, body: { refund_id: "{{ refund.id }}" } } missing: { status: 404, body: { error: unknown order } } failed: { status: 500, rollback: true, body: { error: refund failed } } Key features ¶ Nine engines, one contract code , tool (DB/HTTP/storage/MCP), decide (rules, then a model), llm , loop (bounded tool use), map (a workflow per list item), parallel (different lookups at once), human , and pending contracts. Swap an engine without touching the graph. Deterministic first Every workflow has a determinism profile and a worst-case token cost. Rules decide before models; an unavailable model is an error, never a silent fallback. Durable runs Runs survive restarts, wait for people, pause and resume on any worker, and compensate on rollback. Every run is journaled. Fast where it can be Declared parallel steps run read-only lookups side by side and a step takes as long as its slowest branch; an llm answer can stream to the user as it is written, without changing the result you validate. Memory you can govern An agent can remember a person across sessions: the owner is chosen in YAML, never by the model, recalled text is fenced as data, secure fields are refused, and the cost is bounded before it runs. Forget one memory or one person from Insight or tuvl prune memory . Record, replay, test Pin any run as a fixture and replay it with zero tokens. Offline tests with typed mocks; calibrated, cached judges for free-text checks. Spec-driven Write intent in a spec; analysis proposes contracts and a task plan; codegen, validation and task status are deterministic. Coding agents use the same tools over MCP. Insight Specs and task board, a canvas over the same YAML, runs with breakpoints, step mode and approvals, change-engine checks, judge calibration. REST, SSE and MCP Typed OpenAPI from contracts, journal events over SSE, workflows as MCP tools, and a typed TypeScript client. Governed Ed25519-signed JWTs, default-deny triggers, approvals without self-approval, secure fields kept away from models, policy checked before you ship. Where to start ¶ Installation and the Quickstart The Agentic Manual — the complete document contract Spec-driven development and building with coding agents Engines , Runtime and journal , Insight AI agent instructions ¶ ⬇️ Download AGENTS.md — the rules for coding agents working in a tuvl project ⬇️ Download skills.zip — the tuvl 2.0 skill set (unzip to .agents/skills/ ; tuvl update skills does this for you) License ¶ tuvl is open source software licensed under the Apache License, Version 2.0 .

docs.text: Contributing ¶ Thank you for your interest in contributing to tuvl! By taking part you agree to the Code of Conduct . Before you start ¶ A bug fix or a small improvement: open a pull request. A new feature, or a change to behaviour: open an issue first and describe what you need. Document kinds, engines and artifact types are closed sets, so a design discussion comes before code. A security problem: do not open an issue; follow the security policy . Development setup ¶ Prerequisites ¶ Python 3.13 or 3.14 (see Installation → Troubleshooting ) uv PostgreSQL 16+ with pgvector, and Redis Node.js 20+ and pnpm (Insight) Install and run ¶ git clone https://github.com/tuvl-io/tuvl.git && cd tuvl uv sync --extra standard --group dev make ui-install uv run tuvl init demo --sample -y uv run tuvl dev -d demo --auto-login # Insight at http://localhost:8885/insight The repository's AGENTS.md maps the code: src/tuvl/contract/ (document model, type and expression languages), validate/ , runtime/ (durable runner, engines, journal), api/ (REST, SSE, MCP, dev API), spec/ , codegen/ , lock/ , testing/ , cli/ , core/ (config, models, auth, artifacts), and ui/ (Insight). Checks ¶ make check # ruff format + lint on src/ make typecheck-gate # mypy on the gated packages (must stay clean) TUVL_TEST_PG_URL=postgresql+asyncpg://tuvl:tuvl@localhost:5432/tuvl_test uv run pytest cd ui && pnpm exec tsc -b && pnpm test # Insight unit tests scripts/insight-smoke.sh # Insight browser tests (Playwright), needs a built UI and Postgres Tests that need Postgres skip without TUVL_TEST_PG_URL . CI runs all of the above. Changing behaviour ¶ The 2.0 specification is the contract: a change to a document kind, engine, signal or validation rule updates the schema ( contract/schema.py ), tuvl lint project , codegen, Insight, the docs and the changelog together. Engines, document kinds and artifact types are closed sets — open an issue before proposing one. Add a test for every fix; prefer real Postgres over mocks for runtime behaviour. Keep comments to the non-obvious why . Pull Request Process ¶ Fork the repository Create a branch for your feature: git checkout -b feature/my-feature Make your changes with clear commit messages, each signed off Add tests for new functionality Run tests to ensure everything passes Submit a PR with a clear description, linking the issue it closes A maintainer reviews the pull request on the repository. tuvl is developed in a private repository and each release is published as a tagged snapshot, so a merged change is applied there and appears in the next tagged release; it keeps your authorship. Sign your commits ¶ tuvl uses the Developer Certificate of Origin : you certify that you wrote the change, or have the right to submit it, under the project's license. Add a Signed-off-by line to each commit with git commit -s . A pull request whose commits are not signed off will be asked to add it ( git rebase --signoff main ). Commit Messages ¶ Use conventional commits: feat: add an http_<status> route for tool agents fix: decide rules type-check enum literals docs: update workflow configuration guide test: cover per-run transactions refactor: simplify repository pattern The repository's pull request template lists the checks (tests, docs, sign-off) a reviewer looks for. Documentation ¶ The site ( tuvl.dev ) is MkDocs Material in the docs repository. The engine's docs/*.md are the source of the Guide pages; make sync-internals copies them into the site. uv sync && uv run mkdocs serve uv run mkdocs build --strict Getting Help ¶ Issues : GitHub Issues Anything else : developer@tuvl.io License ¶ By contributing, you agree that your contributions are licensed under the Apache License, Version 2.0 , and your sign-off certifies the DCO. You keep the copyright in your contribution.

docs.text: What's new in 2.0 ¶ tuvl 2.0.0 is a redesign: workflows are graphs of typed agents , every run is durable and journaled , and projects are built spec-first . There is no 1.x compatibility layer — 1.x workflows fail to load with an error pointing at the 2.0 format. The full list of changes is in the changelog . License: Apache 2.0 tuvl is licensed under the Apache License, Version 2.0 , which includes an express patent grant. Using, modifying and selling software built on tuvl is free. The license New in 2.0.0b10 ¶ Answers that stream llm: { stream_tokens: true } sends the text of one output field to the run's event stream while the model writes it. The result, validation, token count and retries are the same as without it; a rejected or retried answer tells the client to drop the draft; and the validator refuses it next to an output guardrail, because text a guardrail could still refuse must not be shown. Insight shows the draft under the running step, and @tuvl/client has handle.onToken(...) . Existing clients are unchanged: drafts come only with ?drafts=true . API , Engines Steps that run side by side The new parallel engine runs two to sixteen read-only branches (database reads, HTTP GETs, storage reads, llm , read-only code ) at the same time and joins their outputs, so a step takes as long as its slowest branch. The branches are declared in the YAML, checked before anything runs (V040-V042), priced as the sum of their budgets, journaled branch by branch and mocked one by one in offline tests; a worker killed mid-fan-out is resumed on another. A loop also runs the read-only tool calls of one model turn together. Engines Agents that remember, under your rules llm.memory and loop.memory put an owner's earlier turns into the prompt and store the result afterwards. The owner is the signed-in user, the tenant or a named input, chosen in YAML and never by the model; recalled text is fenced as data; secure fields are refused; the recalled tokens count against the policy's cost cap; and every recall is journaled. A person can be forgotten ( tuvl prune memory , or a button in Insight), and retention and tuvl.memory_compact keep it small. Engines , Memory in Insight A Memory page and a parallel step in Insight Browse what agents remember, per collection and owner, and forget one memory or one person. The canvas has a Run lookups in parallel preset, and the run timeline names each branch with its time. Insight Skills for what b8 and b9 added The coding-agent skill set now covers triggers, file uploads, webhooks and per-signal outputs ( tuvl-workflow ), the collection tool, and the new streaming, parallel and memory features. tuvl update skills adds them to a project. New in 2.0.0b9 ¶ Collections in workflows A loop agent can search a collection as a tool ( - collection: kb_docs ): the model supplies the query, and top_k and the filter are fixed in the YAML. In Insight the vector search and ingest steps pick their collection from the configured ones, and a Retrieve and answer step adds a search routed into an answering model that cites its sources. Loop and tools , Embeddings & Collections A better agent panel in Insight An llm or loop agent picks its AI model from the configured presets, takes its prompt, steering, skills, MCP servers and judge from stored artifacts pinned to a version, and the whole agent can be edited as YAML. Insight Ideas from Insight Upload an idea (files, a folder or text) on the Ideas page and generate a spec from it with your coding agent, after asking for consent. Authoring Provenance on PyPI tuvl and tuvl-insight are published with PEP 740 attestations again, and the release fails if PyPI has none for any file. New in 2.0.0b8 ¶ Commands are actions: tuvl <verb> <thing> The pipeline reads in order: init , import idea , generate spec , approve spec , generate tasks , generate code , verify spec , run tests , ship . Each verb makes one promise: generate writes files, lint runs static rules, verify checks that two things are in step, check asks whether something works now, list and show only read. The earlier names are gone; run tuvl generate code once after upgrading. Command reference Specs and tasks in Insight and the terminal UI Approve, send back, reopen and derive tasks from Insight or the terminal UI. A task opens in a panel you can drag and pop out, with what it builds, what it waits for and the spec section it came from. Graph draws the tasks as a tree in execution order. A blocked task says why; a failed run keeps a report of every attempt. tuvl show task prints the same. Insight Webhooks and file uploads A workflow can send a signed notification when a run completes, fails or waits for a person, and a trigger can accept multipart/form-data and pass the run a reference, never the bytes. Webhooks , API Production server and keys tuvl serve app shuts down cleanly behind an ingress and exposes only the route groups you choose ( spec.api.expose ). TUVL_SIGNING_KEY is the only name for the signing key; the 1.x TUVL_BISCUIT_PRIVATE_KEY is no longer read. Authentication Nest: the public catalogue Applications built with tuvl can be listed at nest.tuvl.io . tuvl register project shows the exact payload first and asks; sign-in is GitHub's device flow. Run your own with --nest URL or TUVL_NEST_URL . Project and catalogue Tools: Laya Serve and Flightlog A new Tools section. Laya Serve is the container image of the Laya decision model that decide agents can use. Flightlog is the collector for developer telemetry, as a small Python service and as a tuvl project. Developer telemetry (optional) Share what developers do on a project through a collector your team runs, and see what the others did in Insight and with tuvl list team-activity . A token per developer, initials from registration, token rotation, and a private certificate authority. Developer telemetry Failures and branches in Insight A failed task keeps a report of what was tried and why it failed. Tasks are drawn as a graph, and a tree of branches shows parallel work, commits and what should merge first. Long jobs started from Insight survive a reload. Insight Highlights ¶ Authoring with your coding agent, acceptance without one tuvl init finds the agents you have; tuvl import idea numbers an idea, generate spec has your agent draft the spec on a branch, a person approves it, generate tasks derives the tasks, and generate code --spec builds each task on its own pull request. Every step is in a local audit ledger, and tuvl dev shows the path in a terminal UI. Authoring Typed agents, nine engines code , tool (db / http / storage / mcp), decide , llm , loop , map , parallel , human , pending — one contract ( inputs , outputs , signals) for all of them. Named ends replace Response steps. Engines Checked before it runs tuvl lint project checks contracts, data flow, types and policy (V001–V036) and prints each workflow's determinism profile and worst-case token cost. Agentic Manual Durable runtime Runs, journal and checkpoints in Postgres; leases so any worker continues any run; waits for people and tool approvals; compensation; pause, resume, abort, steer; replay. Runtime Rules first, models bounded decide evaluates rules before a decision model and never falls back silently; loop has hard budgets, per-tool approval and a supervisor; judges are calibrated and cached. Decide · Loop and tools · Judges Spec-driven The coding agent builds; tuvl referees. tuvl lint spec checks the spec, tuvl verify spec checks the build against it, and task status is derived, never self-reported. tuvl generate code , tuvl run tests and tuvl generate lock are deterministic; tuvl serve mcp and 14 skills for coding agents. Spec-driven development Fan-out with map engine: map runs a child workflow once for every item of a list, a few at a time. Each item is a run of its own with its own journal, a crashed parent follows the children it already started, and on_error: collect keeps going and routes partial . tuvl lint project prices it at the child's worst case times max_items . Engines Blob storage Named stores in storage/*.yaml for S3 and compatible services, Azure Blob, Google Cloud Storage and local disk, used by tool: { use: storage } and ctx.storage(name) . Built on tuvl's own HTTP client, so no cloud SDK is installed. Keys, prefixes and read-only stores are checked before a run (V030–V034). Blob Storage Insight 2.0 Specs and task board, a canvas over the same YAML, runs with breakpoints and step mode, approvals, change-engine checks against pinned fixtures, judge calibration. Insight REST, SSE, MCP gRPC is gone. OpenAPI is generated from contracts; workflows can be exported as MCP tools; @tuvl/client 2.0 generates typed clients. API Ship and scale tuvl ship gates on validation and the lock, pins the engine version and installs only the features your project uses; the Helm chart can split API and worker pods. Shipping Project identity and the catalogue tuvl init writes .tuvl/project.yaml with a self-checking id, author, type and version. Edit it with tuvl set project or in Insight, and list the project on nest.tuvl.io with tuvl register project or the Register button. Project and Catalogue Verb-first commands Commands read as tuvl <verb> <noun> : tuvl generate code , tuvl list specs , tuvl verify spec , tuvl set project , tuvl review code , tuvl serve app . The server shuts down cleanly on a stop signal. CLI reference Schedules, uploads and webhooks API and schedule triggers are switchable and a scheduled run carries its input ( trigger.schedule: { cron, enabled, input } , validated as V019). The file type and http.upload take multipart uploads (V037). spec.webhooks sends signed, minimal notifications when a run ends. docs.text: tuvl 2.0.0 is a redesign: workflows are graphs of typed agents , every run is durable and journaled , and projects are built spec-first . There is no 1.x compatibility layer — 1.x workflows fail to load with an error pointing at the 2.0 format. The full list of changes is in the changelog . docs.text: Answers that stream llm: { stream_tokens: true } sends the text of one output field to the run's event stream while the model writes it. The result, validation, token count and retries are the same as without it; a rejected or retried answer tells the client to drop the draft; and the validator refuses it next to an output guardrail, because text a guardrail could still refuse must not be shown. Insight shows the draft under the running step, and @tuvl/client has handle.onToken(...) . Existing clients are unchanged: drafts come only with ?drafts=true . API , Engines Steps that run side by side The new parallel engine runs two to sixteen read-only branches (database reads, HTTP GETs, storage reads, llm , read-only code ) at the same time and joins their outputs, so a step takes as long as its slowest branch. The branches are declared in the YAML, checked before anything runs (V040-V042), priced as the sum of their budgets, journaled branch by branch and mocked one by one in offline tests; a worker killed mid-fan-out is resumed on another. A loop also runs the read-only tool calls of one model turn together. Engines Agents that remember, under your rules llm.memory and loop.memory put an owner's earlier turns into the prompt and store the result afterwards. The owner is the signed-in user, the tenant or a named input, chosen in YAML and never by the model; recalled text is fenced as data; secure fields are refused; the recalled tokens count against the policy's cost cap; and every recall is journaled. A person can be forgotten ( tuvl prune memory , or a button in Insight), and retention and tuvl.memory_compact keep it small. Engines , Memory in Insight A Memory page and a parallel step in Insight Browse what agents remember, per collection and owner, and forget one memory or one person. The canvas has a Run lookups in parallel preset, and the run timeline names each branch with its time. Insight Skills for what b8 and b9 added The coding-agent skill set now covers triggers, file uploads, webhooks and per-signal outputs ( tuvl-workflow ), the collection tool, and the new streaming, parallel and memory features. tuvl update skills adds them to a project.

docs.text: Collections in workflows A loop agent can search a collection as a tool ( - collection: kb_docs ): the model supplies the query, and top_k and the filter are fixed in the YAML. In Insight the vector search and ingest steps pick their collection from the configured ones, and a Retrieve and answer step adds a search routed into an answering model that cites its sources. Loop and tools , Embeddings & Collections A better agent panel in Insight An llm or loop agent picks its AI model from the configured presets, takes its prompt, steering, skills, MCP servers and judge from stored artifacts pinned to a version, and the whole agent can be edited as YAML. Insight Ideas from Insight Upload an idea (files, a folder or text) on the Ideas page and generate a spec from it with your coding agent, after asking for consent. Authoring Provenance on PyPI tuvl and tuvl-insight are published with PEP 740 attestations again, and the release fails if PyPI has none for any file.

docs.text: Commands are actions: tuvl <verb> <thing> The pipeline reads in order: init , import idea , generate spec , approve spec , generate tasks , generate code , verify spec , run tests , ship . Each verb makes one promise: generate writes files, lint runs static rules, verify checks that two things are in step, check asks whether something works now, list and show only read. The earlier names are gone; run tuvl generate code once after upgrading. Command reference Specs and tasks in Insight and the terminal UI Approve, send back, reopen and derive tasks from Insight or the terminal UI. A task opens in a panel you can drag and pop out, with what it builds, what it waits for and the spec section it came from. Graph draws the tasks as a tree in execution order. A blocked task says why; a failed run keeps a report of every attempt. tuvl show task prints the same. Insight Webhooks and file uploads A workflow can send a signed notification when a run completes, fails or waits for a person, and a trigger can accept multipart/form-data and pass the run a reference, never the bytes. Webhooks , API Production server and keys tuvl serve app shuts down cleanly behind an ingress and exposes only the route groups you choose ( spec.api.expose ). TUVL_SIGNING_KEY is the only name for the signing key; the 1.x TUVL_BISCUIT_PRIVATE_KEY is no longer read. Authentication Nest: the public catalogue Applications built with tuvl can be listed at nest.tuvl.io . tuvl register project shows the exact payload first and asks; sign-in is GitHub's device flow. Run your own with --nest URL or TUVL_NEST_URL . Project and catalogue Tools: Laya Serve and Flightlog A new Tools section. Laya Serve is the container image of the Laya decision model that decide agents can use. Flightlog is the collector for developer telemetry, as a small Python service and as a tuvl project. Developer telemetry (optional) Share what developers do on a project through a collector your team runs, and see what the others did in Insight and with tuvl list team-activity . A token per developer, initials from registration, token rotation, and a private certificate authority. Developer telemetry Failures and branches in Insight A failed task keeps a report of what was tried and why it failed. Tasks are drawn as a graph, and a tree of branches shows parallel work, commits and what should merge first. Long jobs started from Insight survive a reload. Insight

docs.text: Why tuvl ¶ Intelligent Workflows. Deterministic Execution. tuvl runs typed workflows of agents (code, database and HTTP tools, rules, models, bounded tool loops and people) on a durable, journaled runtime, built from specs. Every route is declared, every model call is budgeted and every run is recorded. The engine refuses anything the contract doesn't declare. This page holds the detail behind the four guarantees on tuvl.io : how execution, data and access are fenced, how tuvl compares with other tools, and what it means for each person who has to say yes. Workflow execution: every path is declared ¶ Nine engines, one contract. Every agent declares typed inputs , outputs and the signals it emits. Its engine is code , tool , decide , llm , loop , map , parallel , human or pending . Custom logic goes into a code agent (a typed Python function), not into the framework. Checked before it runs. tuvl lint project applies 43 rules covering routes, data flow, types, expressions and policy. It prints each workflow's determinism profile and worst-case token cost. Every signal must be routed; there are no implicit edges. tuvl lint spec and tuvl verify spec hold the build to its spec in the same way. Rules before models. A decide agent evaluates its rules first and asks a decision model only when none match. A typed-decision model such as self-hosted Laya returns calibrated probabilities, not text. An unavailable model is an error , never a silent fallback, and a doubtful answer routes low_confidence . Models stay bounded. llm and loop agents must declare token, time and iteration budgets. A model can only pick one of the routes you declared: its choice is constrained to the declared signals, and anything else routes parse_error . Every abnormal exit ( max_iterations , budget_exceeded , timeout , aborted ) is a routable signal. Loops are governed. Tools are agents, child workflows or allow-listed MCP tools, with schemas derived from their contracts. A risky call pauses for a person's approval, a supervisor can pause, steer or abort, and calibrated judges fail closed. Data and state: every access is fenced ¶ Agents see only their inputs. Undeclared context is invisible. An output that doesn't match the contract is a contract_violation , not a surprise further down the workflow. Model allowlist. A workflow can read and write only the models listed in spec.models . This is checked by the validator and again at runtime. Durable by default. Each step's writes commit with its checkpoint. A crashed worker's run resumes from the last checkpoint, and a rollback end compensates completed agents in reverse order. PII never reaches a model. Fields marked secure: true are refused as model inputs at validation, and redacted in the journal and in exports. Reproducible. tuvl.lock pins model ids, artifact hashes and MCP tool schemas. tuvl ship refuses a stale lock and pins the engine version. Security: fail closed, by construction ¶ Callers: no accidental public endpoints ¶ Deny by default. In production, every way to start a run requires a verified token: the workflow's route, the run API and MCP export. This holds even when the YAML declares no scope or group. Forgetting auth config doesn't open an endpoint; it locks one. Public is a declaration, not an omission. trigger.http.public: true is the only way to serve anonymous traffic. Combining it with a required scope or group is a validation error. Gated approvals. A person deciding a human step needs the approvals:decide scope and the step's required_group . On a group-gated step they can't be the person who started the run. Every decision is journaled with who made it. See IAM . Data: read and write are separate grants ¶ CRUD is opt-in. A model gets REST routes only for the operations it lists in spec.api.crud . read , write and delete are independent grants, carried as signed claims in offline-verifiable access tokens (Ed25519 JWTs). Group-pinned models. spec.access can restrict a model to named IAM groups per tier. A caller needs the scope and the membership; the only bypass is the explicit iam:admin grant. Restrictions cascade down, never up. Declare who may read, and the write and delete tiers inherit that fence unless you narrow them further. Surface: the API you don't declare doesn't exist ¶ Kill the CRUD plane entirely. One SystemConfig line unmounts every auto-generated /models/* route. The routes are absent from the router and the OpenAPI schema, rather than hidden behind a 403. No signing key, no boot. A production engine without its signing key refuses to start rather than fall back to anything weaker. Dev conveniences can't leak. The dev-mode superuser shortcut hard-exits the process if it's ever enabled in production. How tuvl compares ¶ Visual flow builders Langflow · Flowise · Dify Code-first frameworks LangGraph · CrewAI · Agents SDK tuvl Source of truth The canvas; exports are JSON blobs Your codebase Specs and YAML in git; Insight's canvas edits the same files What you ship A flow hosted inside the tool A library inside an app you still build A mounted API (routes, models, auth, telemetry), live the day the YAML merges When it breaks At runtime, inside the tool Wherever the Python throws Checked before it runs; declared failures route as signals; a crashed worker's run resumes from its last checkpoint Can the model invent a path? Components are open-ended The graph constrains it; the app around it is code No: it picks from the routes you declared Auth and tenancy The tool's API keys; the rest is yours Bring your own Scoped tokens per route; row-level tenancy Integrations Connector catalogs Ecosystems, plus whatever you write MCP tools in, workflows out as MCP tools; plain HTTP for everything else Lock-in and exit Flows live in the tool's format and runtime A library you can pin, fork or vendor (the cleanest exit here) A YAML dialect you adopt, whose majors land on your calendar too. Apache-2.0 engine; your data stays in your Postgres Path to production Export, then host around it Your Dockerfile, your infra One command to a container and Helm chart ( tuvl ship ) Visual builders are a good canvas for a human exploring. Code-first frameworks are a good library inside an app you own. tuvl is the backend itself, declared. When the closed set isn't enough, a code agent drops to one typed Python function that stays inside the contract: its exits route through declared signals, and its database access stays allowlisted. Who it's for ¶ Engineers: a mechanism you can audit. Typed agent contracts and nine engines form a closed set, checked by 43 validation rules before anything runs. The stack is FastAPI, Postgres with pgvector, a built-in model client for every major provider, and OpenTelemetry. Durable runs are rows in your Postgres, with no extra workflow server and no torch or langchain dependency. Run tuvl dev on a laptop, and tuvl ship for a container and Helm chart. Start with the Agentic Manual . Product managers: scope that ships this sprint. Start from a spec in plain language. The task board's progress is derived from the project, not self-reported. human agents put sign-off inside the workflow: the run waits, durably, for days if needed, and the approval is on record. When someone asks "why did the AI do that?", you open the run and show them. Stakeholders: risk with a fence around it. Apache-2.0 licensed and open source, with no per-seat or per-call platform fee; the only spend is your own infrastructure and model tokens. Your data stays in your Postgres, PII marked secure never reaches a model, and decisions can run on a self-hosted model in your own cluster. The business logic is portable YAML and the runtime is a standard Python wheel, so adopting tuvl doesn't strand you in it. See it built ¶ The examples range from one typed model call (Invoice Extraction API) to durable human review (Content Moderation Pipeline) and a supervised investigation loop with a calibrated judge and group-gated compliance decisions (KYC Onboarding). Or run any of them in a throwaway sandbox at try.tuvl.online .

docs.text: AI Models ¶ An AgentModel (in llms/ ) names a model so workflows can refer to it. There are two types: llm (the default) for llm and loop agents, and judges, and decision for the decide engine. tuvl init --preset gemini|openai|anthropic|ollama writes llms/default.yaml for you. The coding agent that drafts specs and builds tasks is not an AI model of the project: it is the one installed on your machine ( tuvl use agent ), see Authoring with a coding agent . LLM models ¶ kind: AgentModel version: v1 metadata: name: default spec: model: gemini/gemini-3.1-flash-lite # a provider/model id api_key: ${GEMINI_API_KEY} # optional; read from the environment temperature: 0.2 max_tokens: 2048 timeout: 60 Property Description model Model id: provider/model (required) — see Models and Providers api_base Endpoint, for Ollama, a gateway or any OpenAI-compatible server api_key Use ${ENV_VAR} — secrets live in .env , never in YAML. Without it, the provider's standard variable ( OPENAI_API_KEY , ANTHROPIC_API_KEY , GEMINI_API_KEY , …) is used temperature , max_tokens Defaults for calls through this model (an agent's budget.max_tokens still bounds it) timeout Request timeout in seconds (default 60) enabled false disables the model; agents that use it fail loudly instead of falling back Provider Example model Ollama (local) ollama/llama3.1 with api_base: http://localhost:11434 OpenAI openai/gpt-5.4-mini Anthropic anthropic/claude-haiku-4-5 Gemini gemini/gemini-3.1-flash-lite Azure OpenAI azure/<deployment> with AZURE_OPENAI_ENDPOINT or api_base Amazon Bedrock bedrock/<model id> with AWS_BEARER_TOKEN_BEDROCK and AWS_REGION Vertex AI vertex_ai/google/<model> with VERTEX_ACCESS_TOKEN and GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT Cohere, Groq, Mistral, DeepSeek, xAI cohere/… , groq/… , mistral/… , deepseek/… , xai/… LiteLLM proxy or other gateway litellm_proxy/<alias> with api_base and api_key tuvl calls these with its own HTTP client; nothing else is installed. Providers, key variables and caveats: Models and Providers . Decision models ¶ kind: AgentModel metadata: { name: triage-classifier } spec: type: decision provider: llm # laya | jev | llm model: gemini/gemini-3.1-flash-lite A decision model picks one value of a decide agent's enum output with a confidence; it never writes free text. Laya (self-hosted). tuvl init --decision-model laya writes this model, LAYA_API_* entries in .env , and a compose.yaml that runs the laya-serve container on localhost:8000 ( docker compose up -d laya ). tuvl ship adds Laya to the Helm chart ( Shipping to production ). The tuvl/laya-serve image comes in two variants: Tag Checkpoints Memory Use with <version>-en english about 2 GiB model: english <version> english + multilingual about 3.5 GiB model: auto or multilingual tuvl init scaffolds model: english with the -en image, and tuvl ship picks the image (and the Helm memory requests) that matches the model. An -en image has no multilingual weights and runs offline, so non-English text sent to it fails with HTTP 500 inference failed — set model: auto and use the full image when you need other languages. kind: AgentModel metadata: { name: laya } spec: type: decision provider: laya model: english # english | auto | multilingual | typed-decisions api_base: ${LAYA_API_BASE:http://localhost:8000} api_key: ${LAYA_API_KEY:} # optional; an ${ENV_VAR} reference, never a literal key Jev (hosted). provider: jev with its api_base , and model pinned to a version ( jev-1.13.0 ). OpenAI-compatible endpoints (a LiteLLM proxy, your own classifier) use provider: llm with model: openai/<name> , api_base and an ${ENV_VAR} api_key . The endpoint must return {"decision": …, "confidence": 0..1} (or token logprobs); an answer with no confidence is an error, never treated as certain. See Decide . Where models are used ¶ Site Field llm agent llm.model: default (or a provider/model id directly) loop agent loop.model decide agent decide.model.ref — a decision model or an llm model Judge artifact spec.model Model ids are pinned in tuvl.lock by tuvl generate lock . You can also manage models on the Insight AI Models page.

docs.text: An AgentModel (in llms/ ) names a model so workflows can refer to it. There are two types: llm (the default) for llm and loop agents, and judges, and decision for the decide engine. tuvl init --preset gemini|openai|anthropic|ollama writes llms/default.yaml for you. The coding agent that drafts specs and builds tasks is not an AI model of the project: it is the one installed on your machine ( tuvl use agent ), see Authoring with a coding agent .

docs.text: kind: AgentModel version: v1 metadata: name: default spec: model: gemini/gemini-3.1-flash-lite # a provider/model id api_key: ${GEMINI_API_KEY} # optional; read from the environment temperature: 0.2 max_tokens: 2048 timeout: 60 Property Description model Model id: provider/model (required) — see Models and Providers api_base Endpoint, for Ollama, a gateway or any OpenAI-compatible server api_key Use ${ENV_VAR} — secrets live in .env , never in YAML. Without it, the provider's standard variable ( OPENAI_API_KEY , ANTHROPIC_API_KEY , GEMINI_API_KEY , …) is used temperature , max_tokens Defaults for calls through this model (an agent's budget.max_tokens still bounds it) timeout Request timeout in seconds (default 60) enabled false disables the model; agents that use it fail loudly instead of falling back Provider Example model Ollama (local) ollama/llama3.1 with api_base: http://localhost:11434 OpenAI openai/gpt-5.4-mini Anthropic anthropic/claude-haiku-4-5 Gemini gemini/gemini-3.1-flash-lite Azure OpenAI azure/<deployment> with AZURE_OPENAI_ENDPOINT or api_base Amazon Bedrock bedrock/<model id> with AWS_BEARER_TOKEN_BEDROCK and AWS_REGION Vertex AI vertex_ai/google/<model> with VERTEX_ACCESS_TOKEN and GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT Cohere, Groq, Mistral, DeepSeek, xAI cohere/… , groq/… , mistral/… , deepseek/… , xai/… LiteLLM proxy or other gateway litellm_proxy/<alias> with api_base and api_key tuvl calls these with its own HTTP client; nothing else is installed. docs.text: Datasource Configuration ¶ Datasources define database connections for your tuvl application. PostgreSQL Configuration ¶ kind: "DataSource" version: "v1" metadata: name: "main_postgres" primary: true spec: type: "postgresql" driver: "asyncpg" connection: host: "${POSTGRES_HOST}" port: ${POSTGRES_PORT:5432} database: "${POSTGRES_DB}" username: "${POSTGRES_USER}" password: "${POSTGRES_PASSWORD}" pooling: min_size: 5 max_size: 20 Metadata Properties ¶ Property Type Required Description name string Yes Unique identifier for this datasource primary boolean No Mark this as the primary datasource. System tables (IAM, HITL, vector store) and the bootstrap ledger are created here. Only one datasource should be marked primary; if none is marked, the first Postgres datasource loaded is used automatically. Connection Properties ¶ Property Type Required Description host string Yes Database server hostname port integer No Port number (default: 5432) database string Yes Database name username string Yes Connection username password string Yes Connection password Pool Configuration ¶ Property Type Default Description min_size integer 5 Minimum connections to maintain max_size integer 20 Maximum connections allowed Tuning Guidelines ¶ Development : min_size: 2 , max_size: 10 Production : min_size: 5-10 , max_size: 20-50 Keep min_size low to reduce idle resource usage Set max_size based on expected concurrent requests Environment Variables ¶ Create a .env file: POSTGRES_HOST=localhost POSTGRES_PORT=5432 POSTGRES_DB=tuvl POSTGRES_USER=postgres POSTGRES_PASSWORD=your_secret_password And a .env.example for documentation: POSTGRES_HOST=localhost POSTGRES_PORT=5432 POSTGRES_DB=tuvl POSTGRES_USER=postgres POSTGRES_PASSWORD= Multiple Databases ¶ Define multiple datasources for different purposes: kind: "DataSource" version: "v1" metadata: name: "primary" spec: type: "postgresql" driver: "asyncpg" connection: host: "${PRIMARY_DB_HOST}" database: "${PRIMARY_DB_NAME}" username: "${PRIMARY_DB_USER}" password: "${PRIMARY_DB_PASSWORD}" kind: "DataSource" version: "v1" metadata: name: "analytics" spec: type: "postgresql" driver: "asyncpg" connection: host: "${ANALYTICS_DB_HOST}" database: "${ANALYTICS_DB_NAME}" username: "${ANALYTICS_DB_USER}" password: "${ANALYTICS_DB_PASSWORD}" SSL/TLS Configuration ¶ For secure connections: spec: type: "postgresql" driver: "asyncpg" connection: host: "${POSTGRES_HOST}" port: 5432 database: "${POSTGRES_DB}" username: "${POSTGRES_USER}" password: "${POSTGRES_PASSWORD}" ssl: mode: "require" # disable, allow, prefer, require, verify-ca, verify-full ca_cert: "/path/to/ca.crt" Docker Compose Example ¶ version: "3.8" services: postgres: image: postgres:16-alpine environment: POSTGRES_USER: postgres POSTGRES_PASSWORD: postgres POSTGRES_DB: tuvl ports: - "5432:5432" volumes: - postgres_data:/var/lib/postgresql/data app: build: . environment: POSTGRES_HOST: postgres POSTGRES_PORT: 5432 POSTGRES_DB: tuvl POSTGRES_USER: postgres POSTGRES_PASSWORD: postgres depends_on: - postgres volumes: postgres_data: Connection String Format ¶ Internally, tuvl builds a connection string: postgresql+asyncpg://user:password@host:port/database Troubleshooting ¶ Connection Refused ¶ sqlalchemy.exc.OperationalError: connection refused Check PostgreSQL is running: pg_isready -h localhost Verify hostname and port Check firewall rules Authentication Failed ¶ asyncpg.exceptions.InvalidPasswordError: password authentication failed Verify username and password Check pg_hba.conf authentication settings Database Does Not Exist ¶ asyncpg.exceptions.InvalidCatalogNameError: database "tuvl" does not exist Create the database: createdb tuvl # or psql -c "CREATE DATABASE tuvl;" Pool Exhausted ¶ asyncpg.exceptions.TooManyConnectionsError Increase max_size in pool config Check for connection leaks (unclosed sessions) Add connection timeout handling Best Practices ¶ 1. Never Commit Secrets ¶ .env *.pem *.key 2. Use Environment Variables ¶ # Good password: "${POSTGRES_PASSWORD}" # Never do this password: "hardcoded_password" 3. Set Reasonable Pool Limits ¶ pooling: min_size: 5 # Low enough for idle efficiency max_size: 20 # High enough for peak load 4. Use SSL in Production ¶ ssl: mode: "verify-full" ca_cert: "${SSL_CA_PATH}" Redis Configuration ¶ Redis is a second supported datasource type used for distributed state — specifically OAuth CSRF tokens and the token revocation blacklist. kind: DataSource version: v1 metadata: name: redis-primary spec: type: redis connection: host: ${REDIS_HOST:localhost} port: ${REDIS_PORT:6379} db: 0 password: ${REDIS_PASSWORD:} # leave blank for no authentication Redis Connection Properties ¶ Property Type Default Description host string localhost Redis server hostname port integer 6379 Redis server port db integer 0 Database index (0–15) password string (none) AUTH password; omit for unauthenticated connections Selection logic When multiple type: redis datasource files exist, tuvl picks the one that sorts first alphabetically by filename. Name your primary Redis file redis-primary.yaml or 00-redis.yaml to ensure predictable selection. Multi-worker requirement Without a configured and reachable Redis datasource, OAuth state tokens and the token revocation blacklist fall back to in-process memory. This is only safe for single-worker development. For production multi-worker deployments Redis is required . For full details on scaling considerations and Docker setup, see Redis Configuration . Next Steps ¶ Redis — Configure Redis for distributed state Agents — Configure LLM providers Agentic Manual — documents, types and models

docs.text: Configuration Overview ¶ tuvl uses YAML files for all configuration. This keeps your logic declarative and version-controllable. Configuration Types ¶ Kind Directory Purpose ModelDefinition models/ Data model schemas Workflow workflows/ Business logic flows DataSource datasources/ Database connections AgentModel llms/ LLM and decision models Storage storage/ Named blob stores: S3, Azure Blob, GCS, local disk ( Blob Storage ) Artifact artifacts/ Named, versioned assets — prompts, steering, skills, guardrails, hooks, MCP servers — referenced via artifact://name[@version] SystemConfig .tuvl/system.yaml Project-level, boot-time API surface settings Environment Variables ¶ Sensitive values use environment variable substitution: connection: host: "${POSTGRES_HOST}" password: "${POSTGRES_PASSWORD}" Syntax ¶ Pattern Behavior ${VAR} Required — fails if not set ${VAR:default} Optional — uses default if not set ${VAR:-default} Same as above (alternate syntax) Example ¶ spec: connection: host: "${POSTGRES_HOST}" # Required port: ${POSTGRES_PORT:5432} # Default: 5432 database: "${POSTGRES_DB:-tuvl}" # Default: tuvl File Organization ¶ project/ ├── .env # Secret values (git-ignored) ├── .env.example # Template (safe to commit) ├── models/ │ ├── user.yaml │ └── order.yaml ├── workflows/ │ ├── onboarding.yaml │ └── checkout.yaml ├── datasources/ │ └── postgres.yaml └── agents/ └── default.yaml Common Patterns ¶ YAML Anchors ¶ Reduce duplication with anchors: agents: - id: summarise # … budget: &llm_budget { timeout: 30s, max_tokens: 1500, retry: { attempts: 2, errors: [timeout, parse_error] } } - id: reply # … budget: *llm_budget Define the anchor where it is first used: documents are strict, so an extra top-level key just to hold an anchor is rejected. Multi-Document Files ¶ tuvl reads each YAML document separately using yaml.safe_load_all . This lets you pack multiple definitions into a single file — useful for colocating related versions: # models/all.yaml kind: "ModelDefinition" metadata: name: "User" schema_version: "v1" spec: tablename: "users" # ... --- kind: "ModelDefinition" metadata: name: "User" schema_version: "v2" # new version in same file enabled: false # staged — activate via admin API spec: tablename: "users" # ... The same pattern works for Workflow documents. Every version — enabled or disabled — is stored in the corresponding *_VERSION_REGISTRY so the admin API can list, toggle, and fork it. schema_version ¶ metadata.schema_version tags a definition with a version string. It defaults to "v1" when omitted. Multiple definitions sharing the same metadata.name but different schema_version values coexist in the registry independently. enabled ¶ Setting enabled: false excludes a definition from active use (no route mounted, no CRUD endpoints) but keeps it visible and manageable through the admin API. Omitting the field is equivalent to enabled: true . SystemConfig ( .tuvl/system.yaml ) ¶ Boot-time settings that shape the mounted API surface, read once at startup. The only knob today is spec.api.expose_model_crud : kind: SystemConfig metadata: name: system spec: api: expose_model_crud: false # default: true Setting expose_model_crud: false unmounts every auto-generated /models/* CRUD router — the routes are absent entirely, not merely scope-denied — leaving only hand-authored Workflow triggers exposed. Restart required for the change to take effect. TUVL_EXPOSE_MODEL_CRUD overrides the YAML value at the env level (env wins over .tuvl/system.yaml ). In dev mode, the toggle is also editable from the Insight Settings page 's API Access section. See Authorization Surfaces for the CRUD and workflow-trigger auth model this knob sits alongside. Validation ¶ tuvl lint projects configurations at startup. Invalid files are logged and skipped: INFO: 📋 Model loaded: 'User' WARNING: ⚠️ models/broken.yaml: missing required field 'spec.tablename' — skipped INFO: 📋 Model loaded: 'Order' Hot Reloading (Development) ¶ In development mode, configuration changes are detected: tuvl dev --reload Production Disable hot reloading in production for stability. Next Steps ¶ Datasources — Database configuration Agents — LLM provider setup

docs.text: Redis Configuration ¶ Redis is an optional but strongly recommended infrastructure dependency for tuvl. It is used for: Feature Without Redis With Redis OAuth CSRF state tokens In-process dict (single worker only) Shared across all workers Token revocation blacklist In-process dict (single worker only) Shared across all workers When Is Redis Required? ¶ Redis is required for any multi-worker or multi-process deployment. If you run more than one tuvl worker (e.g. tuvl serve app --workers 4 ), there is no shared memory between processes. Without Redis: An OAuth callback routed to a different worker than the one that generated the state will always fail the CSRF check. A token revoked via POST /auth/logout on one worker will still be accepted by all other workers. In single-worker tuvl dev mode Redis is optional — the in-process fallback is sufficient. Configuration ¶ Create a YAML file in your project's datasources/ directory: kind: DataSource version: v1 metadata: name: redis-primary spec: type: redis connection: host: ${REDIS_HOST:localhost} port: ${REDIS_PORT:6379} db: 0 password: ${REDIS_PASSWORD:} # empty string → no AUTH command sent tuvl picks up the first type: redis datasource (sorted alphabetically by name) and attempts to connect at startup. Connection Properties ¶ Property Type Default Description host string localhost Redis server hostname or IP port integer 6379 Redis server port db integer 0 Database index (0–15) password string (none) AUTH password; omit or leave blank for no auth Environment Variables ¶ REDIS_HOST=redis.internal REDIS_PORT=6379 REDIS_PASSWORD=your-redis-password # optional Environment Variable Syntax ¶ The ${VAR:default} syntax used in the YAML is resolved before connecting: Pattern Behaviour ${REDIS_HOST:localhost} Uses REDIS_HOST env var; falls back to localhost ${REDIS_PASSWORD:} Uses REDIS_PASSWORD env var; falls back to empty string (no auth) ${REDIS_HOST} Requires REDIS_HOST to be set — fails startup with a clear error if missing Startup Behaviour ¶ When tuvl starts, it logs one of the following: 🟥 Redis connected: localhost:6379 db=0 (datasource: 'redis-primary') or, if no datasource is configured or connection fails: ℹ️ No Redis datasource configured — OAuth state and token blacklist will use in-process memory (not suitable for multi-worker deployments). or, if the datasource is configured but the server is unreachable: ⚠️ Redis datasource 'redis-primary' (localhost:6379) is unreachable: ... — falling back to in-process memory. tuvl never fails to start due to Redis being unavailable. The fallback is automatic. Redis availability is checked at the point of use via is_redis_available() . Using Redis for Other Purposes ¶ The Redis client is accessible in application code for custom caching or messaging: from tuvl.core.infra.redis import get_redis_client, is_redis_available async def my_function(): if is_redis_available(): redis = get_redis_client() await redis.set("my:key", "value", ex=300) else: # fallback path ... Docker Setup ¶ services: redis: image: redis:7-alpine ports: - "6379:6379" command: redis-server --requirepass "${REDIS_PASSWORD}" volumes: - redis_data:/data tuvl: # ... environment: REDIS_HOST: redis REDIS_PASSWORD: "${REDIS_PASSWORD}" depends_on: - redis volumes: redis_data: Managed Redis Services ¶ Provider Notes AWS ElastiCache Set host to the primary endpoint; use password for auth token Redis Cloud Standard connection; enable TLS if required (not yet built-in; use a tunnel) Upstash REST API not supported; use the standard TCP endpoint Render / Railway Use the internal REDIS_URL ; parse host/port/password from it manually Azure Cache for Redis Use non-TLS port 6379 for simplicity or configure a TLS proxy UI Configuration ¶ Redis can be configured directly from the tuvl UI: Navigate to Settings → Infrastructure → Redis Fill in the host, port, db index, and optional password Click Save — the YAML file will be written to datasources/redis-primary.yaml The status badge shows Configured when the file exists. The actual Redis connectivity is only visible in the server logs at startup.

docs.text: Redis is an optional but strongly recommended infrastructure dependency for tuvl. It is used for: Feature Without Redis With Redis OAuth CSRF state tokens In-process dict (single worker only) Shared across all workers Token revocation blacklist In-process dict (single worker only) Shared across all workers
docs.title: Redis Configuration

docs.text: Redis is required for any multi-worker or multi-process deployment. If you run more than one tuvl worker (e.g. tuvl serve app --workers 4 ), there is no shared memory between processes. Without Redis: An OAuth callback routed to a different worker than the one that generated the state will always fail the CSRF check. A token revoked via POST /auth/logout on one worker will still be accepted by all other workers. In single-worker tuvl dev mode Redis is optional — the in-process fallback is sufficient.
docs.title: When Is Redis Required?

docs.text: Create a YAML file in your project's datasources/ directory: kind: DataSource version: v1 metadata: name: redis-primary spec: type: redis connection: host: ${REDIS_HOST:localhost} port: ${REDIS_PORT:6379} db: 0 password: ${REDIS_PASSWORD:} # empty string → no AUTH command sent tuvl picks up the first type: redis datasource (sorted alphabetically by name) and attempts to connect at startup.

docs.text: Code generation ¶ tuvl generate code writes the parts of a project that follow mechanically from its YAML, so you only write the parts that need judgement. It is deterministic: no model is called, and tuvl never writes function bodies . tuvl generate code # all workflows tuvl generate code triage_ticket # one workflow's stubs, prompts and tests tuvl generate code --check # write nothing; exit 1 if anything would change (the CI gate) Building a whole spec with your coding agent ¶ The commands above are the deterministic part. For an approved spec, tuvl generate code --spec SPEC --all (or --task 3 , --task 1,3 ) goes further: first, with no tokens spent, it writes the models from # Data and a workflow skeleton of pending steps from # Flows , then it asks your installed coding agent to implement each task on its own branch ( feature/TASK-… ), checks it (the step is implemented, lint project and verify spec agree, the Python passes tuvl review code ), and opens a draft pull request, stacked on the previous one. Nothing is merged for you. See Authoring with a coding agent . What it generates ¶ Output Rule agents/_generated/schemas.py <Id>In / <Id>Out models per agent (per-signal variants and <Id>Signal ), plus <Workflow>Input and <Workflow>End . Never hand-edited agents/<run>.py A stub for each code agent when missing; when present, a merge that refreshes the decorator, signature and docstring and keeps your body artifacts/<name>.md A prompt placeholder for an artifact:// that an llm or loop agent references and that does not exist yet decide agents A block with neither rules nor a model gets one never-matching rule per enum value, each marked # TODO tests/<workflow>/<example>.yaml A test per tuvl-example block in the spec. Hand-written tests are never touched The loop for a code agent ¶ Declare the agent in the workflow YAML (or add a step in Insight): its run , inputs , outputs . Run tuvl generate code . You get a typed stub: from __future__ import annotations from tuvl import Ctx, agent from agents._generated.schemas import ScoreTicketIn, ScoreTicketOut @agent("score_ticket") async def score_ticket(inp: ScoreTicketIn, ctx: Ctx) -> ScoreTicketOut: """Score how urgent a ticket is.""" raise NotImplementedError("score_ticket") Replace the raise with your logic. Everything above the body is owned by codegen. Change the contract later (rename an input, add an output) and run tuvl generate code again: the signature and types update, and your body stays. In Insight, choosing the code engine for an agent offers ⌘ Generate stub , which runs the same step, and saving the Python file normalizes the decorator and signature through codegen. Keeping it honest in CI ¶ Generated files are committed, so a contract change that was not regenerated is a failing build: tuvl generate code --check It is one step of the CI gate , alongside tuvl lint project --strict , tuvl verify lock and tuvl run tests --strict . Run tuvl generate code locally and commit the result. Notes ¶ Don't edit agents/_generated/ . It is rewritten on every run. One @agent("run") per contract. If two agents share a run with different contracts, codegen warns and types the function as Any . Coding agents can run it through the dev MCP server: codegen (a dry run) always, and codegen_write with --allow-write . See Build with Coding Agents . See also ¶ Spec-driven development — where codegen sits in the flow Project structure CLI reference

docs.text: Build with coding agents ¶ There are two ways to work with a coding agent, and both stay open: The open path (this page): point your agent (Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, Kiro, …) at the project. It uses the skills and tuvl serve mcp and builds what it likes; tuvl lint project , tuvl verify spec , tuvl ship and CI still decide what is accepted. The driven path: tuvl drives the agent you already have installed, one narrow job at a time on its own branch, from an idea to a packaged project. See Authoring with a coding agent . The rest of this page is the open path. tuvl is designed so a coding agent (Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, Kiro, …) can build a project from a spec without guessing: tuvl tells it the state of the project, and deterministic tools do everything except the parts that need judgement. What a project gives the agent ¶ AGENTS.md at the root and skills in .agents/skills/ (mirrored to .claude/skills/ ), scaffolded by tuvl init and refreshed with tuvl update skills [--diff] : Skill Use it when tuvl-spec writing or changing specs/<name>.md tuvl-plan writing and maintaining the task list from a checked spec tuvl-task-loop always — the core loop for implementing tasks agent-code / agent-tool / agent-llm / agent-loop / agent-decide / agent-human / agent-map / agent-parallel implementing an agent with that engine tuvl-workflow the workflow around the agents: triggers (http, schedule, mcp), file uploads, ends, policy, webhooks, per-signal outputs tuvl-data models, fields, access, CRUD tuvl-test tests, mocks, fixtures, judges tuvl-review reviewing the Python of code agents (the C-rules, then judgement) tuvl-harden changing a working workflow safely tuvl-ship lock, CI gate, shipping ( tuvl ship installs only the tuvl extras the project uses) --json on every read command ( lint project , list tasks , show drift , run tests , list runs , …), with documented schemas. tuvl serve mcp — the same operations as MCP tools over stdio. Connect tuvl serve mcp ¶ { "mcpServers": { "tuvl": { "command": "tuvl", "args": ["mcp", "-d", "."] } } } Read tools: validate , spec_status , spec_diff , get_contract , list_agents , explain_error , get_run , get_run_events , plus spec_check , spec_verify and dry runs of codegen and test . Add --allow-write for codegen_write , run_workflow and pin_fixture . Run tools talk to a running server through TUVL_URL / TUVL_TOKEN . tuvl serve mcp refuses to run in production. The loop ¶ tuvl list tasks --json → the next unblocked task and its target. tuvl generate code → typed schemas and stubs for the target. Implement: the YAML engine block, or the body of a code agent's function. tuvl lint project --json → fix every error on the target. tuvl run tests → the task moves to tested , then done . Repeat until tuvl list tasks --strict passes. Task statuses are derived from the project — an agent never sets them. Generated files ( agents/_generated/ , generated tests, tuvl.lock ) are regenerated, never edited. Downloads ¶ AGENTS.md and skills.zip for agents working outside a tuvl init project.

docs.text: Build a project: from init to ship ¶ This guide builds one small project from an empty folder to a container image, twice over: with a coding agent and by hand . The two tracks end with the same files and the same checks, because in both of them tuvl is the referee . It checks every step without calling a model, so it costs nothing, and it tells you what is left. You will build refund approvals . A customer asks for a refund on an order. A refund of 100 or less is recorded straight away. A larger one waits for a finance lead, who approves or rejects it. The workflow uses no language model, so every check in this guide is offline and free. What you need tuvl installed ( Installation ); uv tool install "tuvl[standard]" . PostgreSQL, only for Run it . Everything before that is offline. Docker, only if you build the image in Ship it . Writing the Dockerfile and chart needs none. For the agent track: a coding agent that reads AGENTS.md (Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, Kiro, ...). The map ¶ # Stage What happens Main command 1 Create A project folder with config, skills and rules tuvl init 2 Spec Intent, data, flow and examples, in one Markdown file tuvl lint spec 3 Data The models the spec names tuvl lint project 4 Workflow The graph of agents tuvl lint project --strict 5 Tasks One task per model, step and example tuvl list tasks 6 Generate and lock Schemas, tests from the examples, the lock tuvl generate code , tuvl generate lock 7 The gate Seven checks that must all pass see below 8 Run The server, a real request, a real approval tuvl dev 9 Change A spec change flows through the checks tuvl show drift 10 Ship Dockerfile, Helm chart, image tuvl ship Who does what The coding agent builds; tuvl referees. In the agent track you write the intent and review the result, and the agent does stages 2 to 6 by running tuvl's commands until they are green. In the manual track you do those stages yourself. Every tab below shows both. Stages 7 to 10 are the same either way. Prefer to start from an idea? This guide writes the spec by hand. If you have a brief (Markdown, PDF or Word, or a web page, Jira issue or GitHub issue given with --url ) and a coding agent installed, tuvl import idea brief.pdf → tuvl generate spec → tuvl approve spec → tuvl generate tasks → tuvl generate code --spec … does stages 2 to 6 with your agent, one pull request per task, and the same gate at the end. See Authoring with a coding agent . 1. Create the project ¶ tuvl init refunds -y --preset ollama cd refunds -y accepts every default. --preset writes llms/default.yaml for the provider you will use later ( gemini , openai , anthropic or ollama ); this project calls no model, so any preset works. Leave out --sample : that flag adds a ready-made triage example, and here you build your own. refunds/ ├── AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md rules for coding agents (CLAUDE.md just points at AGENTS.md) ├── .agents/skills/ 14 skills for coding agents (mirrored to .claude/skills/) ├── pyproject.toml your Python dependencies (uv) ├── .env, .env.example secrets and connection settings (.env is git-ignored) ├── .tuvl/ project identity (project.yaml) and system settings ├── datasources/postgres.yaml the database connection, read from .env ├── llms/default.yaml the model preset ├── models/ workflows/ agents/ artifacts/ federation/ empty, you fill them └── README.md With a coding agent init already gave the agent everything it needs: AGENTS.md holds the non-negotiable rules (never infer project state, never hand-edit generated files, finish every change green), and the skills in .agents/skills/ teach it each stage: tuvl-spec , tuvl-plan , tuvl-task-loop , one skill per engine ( agent-code , agent-tool , agent-llm , agent-loop , agent-decide , agent-human , agent-map ), tuvl-data , tuvl-test , tuvl-harden and tuvl-ship . Give the agent tuvl's own tools by adding the development MCP server to the agent's config: { "mcpServers": { "tuvl": { "command": "tuvl", "args": ["mcp", "-d", "."] } } } It offers validate , spec_check , spec_verify , spec_status , spec_diff , get_contract , list_agents , explain_error , codegen and test , all read-only. Add --allow-write to also allow codegen_write , run_workflow and pin_fixture . Without MCP the agent runs the same commands in a shell with --json . After you upgrade tuvl, tuvl update skills --diff shows what would change in the skills and tuvl update skills applies it. By hand Nothing more to set up. If you do not use a coding agent, tuvl init --no-ai-skills skips the .agents/ directory (the agent rules and skills). 2. Write the spec ¶ The spec is the one document that says what the project is for. tuvl create spec writes a template that already passes the check: tuvl create spec refund-request A spec is Markdown. # Intent and # Policies are prose for people and the agent. Three parts are structured , and tuvl checks them: # Data (the models), # Flows (the steps, routes and ends) and the tuvl-example blocks under # Acceptance (each one becomes a test). The grammar is in Spec-driven development . With a coding agent You decide what ; the agent writes the structured parts with the tuvl-spec skill. Give it the intent in plain words and ask for the spec only: Use the tuvl-spec skill. Write specs/refund-request.md for this: customers request a refund on an order ( order_id , amount , reason ). If the amount is 100 or less, record it. If it is more, a finance lead (group finance_lead , 24 hours) must approve first; rejected or expired means no refund. An unknown order is a 404. Include an example for every end. Do not build anything yet. Run tuvl lint spec until it has no blocking findings, then show me. Review it before anything is built. This is the cheapest place to catch a wrong idea: Does every end have the right HTTP status, and an example ( tuvl lint spec warns with S011 if not)? Who is allowed to call the flow, and who may approve (S010, S013)? Is the threshold the one you meant, and is it in # Policies too? Is every model marked (new) or (existing) correctly? By hand Replace the template with the spec below. It is the whole project in one file. specs/refund-request.md --- name: refund-request owner: payments-team workflow: refund_request --- # Intent Customers ask for a refund on an order. A small refund is recorded straight away; a larger one waits for a finance lead, who approves or rejects it. # Data - **Order** (existing) — `id` (uuid), `total` (numeric; required) - **Refund** (new) — `order_id` (uuid → Order; required), `amount` (numeric; required), `reason` (text), `status` (enum: recorded | approved; required; default recorded) # Flows ## Flow: refund_request Trigger: POST /api/refunds · signed-in Input: `order_id` (uuid), `amount` (float), `reason` (str) Ends: default 201 · unknown_order 404 · rejected 200 · failed 500 - failed: no example — a create on a new row has no conflict to provoke 1. `load_order` — tool db read Order · in `order_id` · out `order` (Order) - not_found → END.unknown_order 2. `check_amount` — decide rules · in `amount` · out `lane` (enum[auto, review]) - `amount <= 100` → auto - otherwise → review - auto → `record_refund` - review → `finance_review` 3. `finance_review` — human group finance_lead · expires 24h · in `amount` · out `approved` (bool) - true → `record_refund` - false, expired → END.rejected 4. `record_refund` — tool db create Refund · in `order_id`, `amount`, `reason` · out `refund` (Refund) - conflict → END.failed # Policies A refund above 100 is never recorded without a finance lead's approval. # Acceptance ```tuvl-example name: a small refund is recorded given: { Order: [{ id: "6f1c0a52-2a8e-4d0b-9a77-0b9d7c2f1e10", total: 120 }] } input: { order_id: "6f1c0a52-2a8e-4d0b-9a77-0b9d7c2f1e10", amount: 40, reason: "Arrived broken." } expect: { end: default, path: [load_order, check_amount, record_refund] } ``` ```tuvl-example name: an unknown order is refused input: { order_id: "11111111-2222-4333-8444-555555555555", amount: 40, reason: "No such order." } expect: { end: unknown_order, path: [load_order] } ``` ```tuvl-example name: a large refund waits for a finance lead given: { Order: [{ id: "6f1c0a52-2a8e-4d0b-9a77-0b9d7c2f1e10", total: 900 }] } input: { order_id: "6f1c0a52-2a8e-4d0b-9a77-0b9d7c2f1e10", amount: 400, reason: "Wrong size." } expect: { end_or_wait: human, path_includes: [check_amount] } ``` ```tuvl-example name: a finance lead rejects a large refund given: { Order: [{ id: "6f1c0a52-2a8e-4d0b-9a77-0b9d7c2f1e10", total: 900 }] } input: { order_id: "6f1c0a52-2a8e-4d0b-9a77-0b9d7c2f1e10", amount: 400, reason: "Wrong size." } mocks: finance_review: { signal: "false", outputs: { approved: false } } expect: { end: rejected, path: [load_order, check_amount, finance_review] } ``` Reading the flow: each numbered line is a step ( id , engine, inputs in , outputs out ), and the indented lines are routes. tool db read Order loads the order and routes not_found to the end unknown_order . decide rules picks a lane from the amount. human group finance_lead waits for a person. tool db create Refund stores the result. failed: no example is a waiver: the spec says on purpose that this end has no example, and a reviewer can see why. Now check it. Nothing is built yet, so the spec is allowed to be ahead of the project: tuvl lint spec specs/refund-request.md ✗ S007 :11 Order is marked (existing) but is not in models/ · WAIVED :21 flow refund_request: end `failed` has no example — a create on a new row has no conflict to provoke ✗ is blocking and ! is a warning. S007 is the next thing to do: the spec says Order already exists, so tuvl expects models/order.yaml . Every finding names a line and a rule; the full list (S001 to S021) is in the spec reference . 3. Data models ¶ With a coding agent Ask for the models with the tuvl-data skill: "Create the models from # Data in the spec." It writes one ModelDefinition per model and runs tuvl lint spec until S007 is gone. By hand Order is an existing table that the flow only reads. Refund is new. kind: ModelDefinition version: v1 metadata: name: Order schema_version: v1 description: A customer order. Already in the database; the refund flow only reads it. spec: tablename: orders fields: - name: id type: uuid primary_key: true - name: total type: numeric required: true kind: ModelDefinition version: v1 metadata: name: Refund schema_version: v1 description: A refund recorded against an order. spec: tablename: refunds api: crud: [list, read] fields: - name: id type: uuid primary_key: true input: false - name: order_id type: uuid required: true - name: amount type: numeric required: true - name: reason type: text - name: status type: enum enum_values: [recorded, approved] default: recorded required: true - name: created_at type: timestamptz input: false A few things worth knowing: input: false keeps a server-generated field out of the create schema, enum_values plus default give the status its starting value, and api: crud: [list, read] exposes read-only routes for refunds (writes go through the workflow). The model YAML has no foreign-key option, so uuid → Order in the spec is checked against a plain uuid field. tuvl lint spec # S007 is gone 4. The workflow ¶ A workflow is a graph of agents . Each agent has a typed contract ( inputs , outputs , the signals it can emit) and an engine that does the work. Routes connect signals to the next agent or to a named end, and there are no implicit edges. Agent Engine What it does load_order tool (db read) Loads the order; not_found ends as unknown_order (404) check_amount decide (rules) amount <= 100 is auto , anything else is review finance_review human Waits for a person in finance_lead ; false or expired ends as rejected record_refund tool (db create) Writes the refund; a conflict ends as failed With a coding agent The agent builds the workflow with the tuvl-task-loop skill, one task at a time, and picks the engine skill for each step ( agent-tool , agent-decide , agent-human ). The loop it follows is the same one you would: tuvl list tasks --json says which task is next and why others are blocked. Build what the task targets, exactly as the spec line says. tuvl generate code after any contract change. tuvl lint project --json and tuvl verify spec --json ; fix every error. tuvl run tests --json until a passing test goes through the step. Repeat until tuvl list tasks --strict exits 0. A step it cannot finish stays pending (a contract with no implementation) instead of being faked. Only a code agent needs Python, and then only the function body. Review the diff. Compare workflows/refund_request.yaml with the spec line by line. tuvl spec verify does the same comparison for you (stage 7), but a person should still read it once. By hand workflows/refund_request.yaml kind: Workflow version: tuvl/v2 metadata: name: refund_request description: Record a refund; a large one waits for a finance lead. spec: models: [Order, Refund] trigger: http: { path: /api/refunds, method: POST } input: order_id: uuid amount: float reason: str agents: - id: load_order description: Load the order being refunded engine: tool inputs: { order_id: uuid } outputs: { order: Order } tool: use: db model: Order op: read where: { id: "{{ order_id }}" } routes: default: check_amount not_found: END.unknown_order error: END.failed - id: check_amount description: A refund of 100 or less is recorded straight away; a larger one needs a lead engine: decide inputs: { amount: float } outputs: { lane: "enum[auto, review]" } decide: rules: - { when: "amount <= 100", then: auto } - { when: "true", then: review } routes: auto: record_refund review: finance_review error: END.failed - id: finance_review description: A finance lead approves or rejects a large refund engine: human inputs: { amount: float } outputs: { approved: bool } human: title: "Refund of {{ amount }}" instruction: Approve to record this refund. show: [amount] required_group: finance_lead expires: 24h route_on: approved routes: "true": record_refund "false": END.rejected expired: END.rejected error: END.failed - id: record_refund description: Record the refund engine: tool inputs: { order_id: uuid, amount: float, reason: str } outputs: { refund: Refund } tool: use: db model: Refund op: create values: order_id: "{{ order_id }}" amount: "{{ amount }}" reason: "{{ reason }}" routes: default: END conflict: END.failed error: END.failed outputs: default: status: 201 body: { id: "{{ refund.id }}", amount: "{{ refund.amount }}", status: "{{ refund.status }}" } unknown_order: status: 404 body: { error: no such order } rejected: status: 200 body: { status: rejected } failed: status: 500 body: { error: the refund could not be recorded } Points to notice: routes lists every signal an agent can emit. tuvl lint project rejects a missing route, so a path you forgot is an error, not a surprise at run time. decide rules are { when, then } , first match wins, and the last rule is when: "true" . human has required_group , an expires , and route_on: approved , which turns the boolean answer into the routes "true" and "false" (quoted, they are YAML strings). outputs maps each end to a status and a body. default is the success end. tuvl lint project --strict Models detected: 2 Order, Refund Code agents: none Errors: 0 Warnings: 0 refund_request 4 agents · 3 deterministic · 1 external · worst-case 0 tok needs models: none — no LLM or decision model required ✓ Validation passed — project looks good! The summary line is the determinism profile : three agents are deterministic, one waits for a person (external), and the worst-case token cost is 0 because no model is involved. When you add an llm step later, this line grows a token budget you set. A typo is caught here, not in production Writing a decide rule as - when: "amount <= 100" with value: auto (instead of then: auto ) fails with [V001] spec.agents[check_amount].decide.rules[0].then: Field required . Every error carries a code; tuvl lint project lists them all, and the agent's explain_error tool explains one. 5. The task list ¶ The task list is how tuvl measures progress. It has one task per new model , per step and per example , plus a manual task for anything only a person can do (credentials for an HTTP or MCP step). tuvl never plans with a model, and it never lets anyone set a status: a task's status is derived from the project. Status Means todo Not built yet (a pending agent, a missing file, an example with no test) in_progress Built, but lint project or verify spec reports a problem implemented Validates cleanly and matches the spec tested A passing test covers it done Nothing blocks shipping With a coding agent The agent writes specs/refund-request.tasks.yaml with the tuvl-plan skill, after the spec has no blocking findings. Check its work: every model, step and example should have a task, and no task carries an estimate or a hand-set status (P004). By hand The only values you cannot invent are the hashes . They tie a task to the exact version of the spec section it came from, and tuvl prints them: tuvl lint spec --json | jq -r '.specs[0].hash' # the spec's hash tuvl lint spec --json | jq -r '.specs[0].sections[] | "\(.anchor) \(.hash)"' intent 7ac196eddd46 data 38fe48d961df flows 7d14b7826850 flow-refund-request d4288ac72c9b policies 45985c2e44d8 acceptance d955f6a357cf Put the spec hash in metadata.spec_hash , and each task's section anchor and hash in its spec_ref . The file has nine tasks: the Refund model ( Order is existing, so it needs no task), the four steps and the four examples. specs/refund-request.tasks.yaml kind: TaskPlan version: tuvl/v2 metadata: { name: refund-request, spec: specs/refund-request.md, spec_hash: f010f2617b63 } spec: tasks: -
