The hashes come from the exact text of the spec: if you type the spec above unchanged, the task list passes as printed, and any edit to a section changes its hash (and is reported as P005 until you refresh it, as in stage 9 ). Look at the board: tuvl list tasks Before the tests exist it shows exactly what is missing and why, for example: T1 implemented Refund model tuvl.lock is missing T2 implemented blocked Load the order (tool db read) no passing Test covers refund_request.load_order waiting on T1 T6 todo blocked Example: a small refund is recorded no generated test for example 'a small refund is recorded' — run tuvl generate code waiting on T5 The reasons are the to-do list. The next stage clears them. 6. Generate and lock ¶ tuvl generate code tuvl generate lock + agents/_generated/schemas.py + tests/refund_request/a-small-refund-is-recorded.yaml + tests/refund_request/an-unknown-order-is-refused.yaml + tests/refund_request/a-large-refund-waits-for-a-finance-lead.yaml + tests/refund_request/a-finance-lead-rejects-a-large-refund.yaml 5 file(s) written. wrote tuvl.lock: 0 model(s), 0 artifact(s), 0 judge(s), 0 MCP tool(s) tuvl generate code writes what follows mechanically from your YAML and spec: typed schemas for every agent ( agents/_generated/schemas.py ), and one test per tuvl-example in the spec. It never writes a function body. If the project had a code agent it would also write its stub and keep your code on every later run ( Code generation ). Never edit generated files; change the spec and run it again. tuvl generate lock writes tuvl.lock : the tuvl version and, when you have them, the exact model ids, prompt hashes and MCP tool schemas the project depends on. It is empty of those here, and it still matters: tuvl ship refuses a stale lock (V024), so a model upgrade can never reach production by accident. Commit it. 7. The gate ¶ Seven commands decide whether the project is consistent. Run them together; this is also your CI: tuvl lint spec && tuvl lint project --strict && tuvl generate code --check && tuvl verify lock \ && tuvl run tests --strict && tuvl verify spec --strict && tuvl list tasks --strict Command It proves tuvl lint spec The spec is complete and consistent (S001 to S016) and the task list matches it (P001 to P005) tuvl lint project --strict The workflows are well-formed: routes, types, data flow, policy (V001 to V036). --strict makes warnings fail tuvl generate code --check Generated files are up to date; exits 1 if anything would change tuvl verify lock tuvl.lock matches the project tuvl run tests --strict The tests pass; --strict also fails a result that only passed through unimplemented steps tuvl verify spec --strict The workflow matches the spec step by step (R001 to R010) tuvl list tasks --strict Every task is done $ tuvl run tests --strict PASS a-finance-lead-rejects-a-large-refund (refund_request → END.rejected, 0 tok) PASS a-large-refund-waits-for-a-finance-lead (refund_request → END.?, 0 tok) PASS a-small-refund-is-recorded (refund_request → END.default, 0 tok) PASS an-unknown-order-is-refused (refund_request → END.unknown_order, 0 tok) 4 passed · 0 stubbed (not counted) · 0 failed $ tuvl verify spec --strict refund_request load_order tool db read Order :23 ✓ 4 passed check_amount decide rules :25 ✓ 3 passed finance_review human group finance_lead :30 ✓ mocked in 1 record_refund tool db create Refund :33 ✓ 1 passed 0 mismatch(es) · steps implemented 4/4 · exercised by real tests 3/4 $ tuvl list tasks --strict T1 done Refund model ... T9 done Example: a finance lead rejects a large refund tests 4/4 passing · tuvl.lock current Two details are worth understanding: Tests run offline against an in-memory database. They mock only what is non-deterministic, external or human. Here that is the finance_review step, because nobody answers a form in a test. Business logic ( tool db , decide rules, code ) runs for real, and the order is seeded with given: in the example. That is why verify spec says 3/4 are exercised by real tests: the fourth is mocked on purpose. A mock cannot hide a gap. If a step is still pending , a test that passes through it is reported STUBBED , does not count, and fails --strict . With a coding agent The agent runs this gate after every change and does not stop until it is green. Run it yourself once at the end; that is your acceptance test of the agent's work. By hand If a command fails, its output names the rule and the line. Fix that, and rerun the gate. The troubleshooting table lists the messages you are most likely to meet. 8. Run it ¶ So far nothing needed a database. To call the workflow you need PostgreSQL. Create a database and point .env at it: createdb refunds POSTGRES_HOST=localhost POSTGRES_PORT=5432 POSTGRES_DB=refunds POSTGRES_USER=postgres POSTGRES_PASSWORD=... Start the engine in dev mode: tuvl dev --show-key It prints a security key and the address of Insight, the browser UI ( http://localhost:8885/insight/ ). In dev mode the key works as an admin bearer token. Insight shows the workflow as a graph, runs it with Run , and lists approvals under Runs . On startup tuvl creates the tables for your models; the Order table stands in for the one your system already has, so add an order to refund: export KEY=<the security key> psql refunds -c "insert into orders (id, total) values ('6f1c0a52-2a8e-4d0b-9a77-0b9d7c2f1e10', 900)" A small refund is recorded at once: curl -s -X POST localhost:8885/api/refunds \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $KEY" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{"order_id":"6f1c0a52-2a8e-4d0b-9a77-0b9d7c2f1e10","amount":40,"reason":"Arrived broken."}' HTTP 201 {"id":"7150932f-1f44-4826-af70-d4d5dcef22b4","amount":40.0,"status":"recorded"} An unknown order takes the unknown_order end: HTTP 404 {"error":"no such order"} A large refund ( "amount":400 ) stops at finance_review . The response is 202 with a run descriptor instead of a refund: HTTP 202 {"run_id":"97b2631a-…","workflow":"refund_request","status":"waiting_human", "current_agent":"finance_review","tokens_used":0, "approval":{"approval_id":"7a1939d5-…","kind":"human","required_group":"finance_lead", "title":"Refund of 400.0","form":{"approved":{"type":"bool","required":true}}}, ...} The run is parked in the database, so it survives a restart. Now approve it. Try with the same key: curl -s -X POST localhost:8885/api/approvals/$APPROVAL_ID \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $KEY" -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"values":{"approved":true}}' HTTP 403 {"detail":"the principal who triggered this run cannot approve it"} That is a deliberate rule: nobody approves their own run . The approver is a different user who holds the approvals:decide scope in the step's group. Create that person (this is also what the IAM page in Insight does). The first administrator comes from POST /auth/bootstrap , which works only while there are no users: B=localhost:8885 curl -s -X POST $B/auth/bootstrap -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{"email":"admin@example.com","password":"<a strong password>","first_name":"Ada","last_name":"Admin"}' AT=$(curl -s -X POST $B/auth/token -d "username=admin@example.com&password=<a strong password>" | jq -r .access_token) A=(-H "Authorization: Bearer $AT" -H "Content-Type: application/json") ROLE=$(curl -s -X POST $B/auth/admin/roles "${A[@]}" \ -d '{"name":"finance_lead","scopes":["approvals:decide","runs:read"]}' | jq -r .id) USER=$(curl -s -X POST $B/auth/admin/users "${A[@]}" \ -d '{"email":"lead@example.com","password":"<another password>","first_name":"Lee","last_name":"Lead"}' | jq -r .id) curl -s -X POST $B/auth/admin/users/$USER/roles/$ROLE "${A[@]}" # 204 Role names become the token's groups , which is how required_group: finance_lead finds them. Now the lead signs in, sees the approval and decides: LT=$(curl -s -X POST $B/auth/token -d "username=lead@example.com&password=<another password>" | jq -r .access_token) L=(-H "Authorization: Bearer $LT" -H "Content-Type: application/json") curl -sL $B/api/approvals/ "${L[@]}" # the lead's inbox curl -s -X POST $B/api/approvals/$APPROVAL_ID "${L[@]}" -d '{"values":{"approved":true}}' The run continues from where it stopped and finishes on the default end: curl -s $B/api/runs/$RUN_ID -H "Authorization: Bearer $KEY" | jq -c '{status, end, output}' {"status":"completed","end":"default","output":{"body":{"id":"3ad7dbf2-…","amount":400.0,"status":"recorded"},"status":201}} TUVL_URL=http://localhost:8885 TUVL_TOKEN=$KEY tuvl list runs # every run, with its end tuvl follow run <run_id> # follows a run until it ends (Ctrl-C to stop) Every step of every run is journaled, so you can see what happened and replay it. Open Insight ( http://localhost:8885/insight/ ) to look at the same project: Specs is the task board from stage 5: nine tasks, all in Done . Workflows → refund_request draws the graph ( load_order , check_amount , the orange finance_review and record_refund , and the four ends) and repeats the profile: 4 agents · 3 deterministic · 1 external · worst-case 0 tok . Runs lists every run. Open the parked one to see the approval form and the journal: load_order → default , check_amount decided review by rule#2 , finance_review approval requested . Submitting the form as the user who started the run shows the same refusal as the API. After the lead decides, the journal adds approval decided by … , resumed and run completed END.default (201) with the response, and Pin as fixture turns the run into a test that replays with zero tokens. The parked run is a row in your database, so it also survives restarting the engine: stop tuvl dev , start it again, and the run is still waiting_human . Dev keys are for development In production there is no session key: callers use signed tokens, and trigger.http.public: true is the only way to open a route without one. See Authentication . 9. Change it later ¶ The spec stays the source of truth. Suppose finance raises the automatic limit from 100 to 200. Change the spec first (the flow's rule and the policy), and let tuvl show you what moved: tuvl lint spec ! P005 specs/refund-request.tasks.yaml:11 T2: spec section #flow-refund-request changed since the task was written ! P005 specs/refund-request.tasks.yaml:17 T3: ... 0 blocking · 4 warning(s) tuvl verify spec check_amount decide rules :25 ✗ mismatch 3 passed ✗ R007 :25 `check_amount`: the workflow's rules differ from the spec's tuvl show drift lists the stale tasks and the spec sections no task covers. Now the work is clear: the workflow still says 100, and four tasks point at a section that changed. With a coding agent Say it in terms of the spec, and let the agent follow the loop: Finance raised the automatic limit from 100 to 200. Update the spec (the flow rule and the policy) and add an example for a refund of 150. Then bring the task list and the workflow back in line and run the full gate. Do not change the workflow before the spec. The tuvl-plan skill tells it to refresh the spec_ref hashes it has reviewed, to add tasks for new steps and to mark removed ones obsolete: true rather than delete them. By hand Change the rule in workflows/refund_request.yaml to amount <= 200 , then refresh the hashes in the task list from tuvl lint spec --json (the same commands as stage 5), and rerun the gate: tuvl lint spec && tuvl verify spec --strict && tuvl run tests --strict && tuvl list tasks --strict All four commands exit 0 again. The order matters: spec first, then the workflow . If you change the workflow first, verify spec reports a contradiction until the spec catches up. 10. Ship it ¶ When the gate is green, shipping is one command. In CI, run the gate on every pull request (this is the exact gate the example projects use): name: CI gate on: [push, pull_request] jobs: gate: runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: - uses: actions/checkout@v4 - uses: astral-sh/setup-uv@v5 - name: Install tuvl run: uv tool install --python 3.13 "tuvl[standard]>=2.0.0,<3" - name: Gate run: | tuvl lint spec tuvl lint project --strict tuvl generate code --check tuvl verify lock --no-mcp tuvl run tests --strict tuvl verify spec --strict tuvl list tasks --strict Then: tuvl generate key --write # a persistent signing key for production tokens tuvl ship -t registry.example.com/refunds:1.0 # add --push to push, --no-build to skip docker Step 1/3 — validate ✓ Validation passed ✓ tuvl.lock is current (tuvl 2.0.0) ✓ tuvl extras: none — the base install is enough not installed: mcp, redis, vector, otel-grpc Step 2/3 — deploy artifacts wrote deploy/Dockerfile wrote .dockerignore wrote deploy/chart/refunds/Chart.yaml ... image contents: 16 file(s) — agents/ 2, models/ 3, workflows/ 2, tuvl.lock, ... Step 3/3 — container image tuvl ship runs the same validation first, so nothing ships that does not validate: no pending agents (V010), a current lock (V024), no development files in the image (V027). It then writes: deploy/Dockerfile , pinned to the tuvl version in tuvl.lock , installing only the extras your project uses. This one needs none, so the image carries the bare install (about 65 MB of Python packages). A .dockerignore that is an allowlist : only the project's models, workflows, agents, datasources, tuvl.lock and runtime config enter the image. Specs, tests, task lists, .env and the agent skills stay out. A Helm chart in deploy/chart/refunds/ , with an optional split into API and worker pods. Deploy it with the tools you already have: kubectl create secret generic refunds-env --from-env-file=.env helm install refunds deploy/chart/refunds --set image.repository=registry.example.com/refunds # separate API and worker pods: helm upgrade refunds deploy/chart/refunds --set split=true --set worker.replicaCount=3 The secret must hold TUVL_SIGNING_KEY (from tuvl generate key ), POSTGRES_PASSWORD , and the variable of every model the workflows use (none here). A production engine refuses to start while one is missing. The container runs in production mode: no dev routes, no Insight, JSON logs. The chart does not include Postgres, so point POSTGRES_HOST at yours. More: Shipping to production . tuvl deploy is coming A hosted, managed tuvl engine that runs your backend services is planned, so there is no image or cluster to operate. tuvl deploy is the command for it. It is not available yet: today it prints a message, deploys nothing and exits 1. Until then, tuvl ship plus helm is the way. Optional: list it in the catalogue ¶ Every project already carries an identity file, .tuvl/project.yaml , with a stable id and your git name and email. If you want the project listed in the public catalogue at nest.tuvl.io, look first: tuvl show project tuvl set project description "Refund approvals: small refunds at once, large ones wait for a lead." tuvl register project # prints the exact payload and asks; answer n to only look Registering is public and is tied to the GitHub account you sign in with. The author name in the listing is your git name , so check it first ( tuvl set project author "…" ). Your email stays private unless you add --public-email , and nothing about your workflows, models or data is sent. If you use a coding agent, it will not register on its own: it only does so when you ask. Details, every field and the error messages: Project and Catalogue . test for example '...' — run tuvl generate code The example has no test yet tuvl generate code tuvl.lock is missing / [V024] tuvl.lock is out of date The lock does not match the project or the installed tuvl tuvl generate lock , review, commit P005 spec section ... changed since the task was written The spec moved after the task list was written Update the tasks and refresh their hashes R007 the workflow's rules differ from the spec's The workflow and the spec disagree Change the spec first, then the workflow STUBBED in tuvl run tests --strict The test only passed through a pending agent Implement the agent 403 the principal who triggered this run cannot approve it You approved your own run Approve as another user in the step's group Ship aborted — the kept Dockerfile does not install tuvl[...] The project now needs an extra the old Dockerfile lacks tuvl ship --force needs the 'codegen' extra: pip install 'tuvl[codegen]' A development command on a bare install Install tuvl[standard] Cheat sheet ¶ I want to Run Start a project tuvl init <name> -y --preset <provider> Start a spec tuvl create spec <name> (or tuvl import idea <brief> then tuvl generate spec ) Approve a spec / derive its tasks tuvl approve spec <spec> / tuvl generate tasks <spec> Build the tasks with your coding agent tuvl generate code --spec <spec> --all Review the agents' Python tuvl review code ( --agent for a second opinion) See what was done to the project tuvl show audit (or Insight → Audit) Check the spec / the build against it tuvl lint spec / tuvl verify spec See what to do next tuvl list tasks ( --json for agents) See what changed since the plan tuvl show drift Generate schemas, stubs, tests tuvl generate code ( --check in CI) Check the workflows tuvl lint project --strict Run the tests tuvl run tests --strict Pin models and tools tuvl generate lock ( --check in CI) Run it locally tuvl dev --show-key Look at runs tuvl list runs , tuvl follow run <id> Serve it to a coding agent tuvl serve mcp Package it tuvl ship -t <image> ( --format archive for a zip/tar you run with uv ) Look at, edit or publish the project's identity tuvl show project , tuvl set project , tuvl register project Where next ¶ Quickstart : the same flow on the built-in triage sample, which includes an llm step. Spec-driven development : the full grammar and every rule code. Engines : code , tool , decide , llm , loop , map and human in depth. Build with coding agents : the skills and the MCP server. Shipping to production : extras, the chart, Laya, Redis and storage.
docs.title: Guide: Init to Ship

docs.text: This guide builds one small project from an empty folder to a container image, twice over: with a coding agent and by hand . The two tracks end with the same files and the same checks, because in both of them tuvl is the referee . It checks every step without calling a model, so it costs nothing, and it tells you what is left. You will build refund approvals . A customer asks for a refund on an order. A refund of 100 or less is recorded straight away. A larger one waits for a finance lead, who approves or rejects it. The workflow uses no language model, so every check in this guide is offline and free. What you need tuvl installed ( Installation ); uv tool install "tuvl[standard]" . PostgreSQL, only for Run it . Everything before that is offline. Docker, only if you build the image in Ship it . Writing the Dockerfile and chart needs none. For the agent track: a coding agent that reads AGENTS.md (Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, Kiro, ...).
docs.title: Build a project: from init to ship

docs.text: # Stage What happens Main command 1 Create A project folder with config, skills and rules tuvl init 2 Spec Intent, data, flow and examples, in one Markdown file tuvl lint spec 3 Data The models the spec names tuvl lint project 4 Workflow The graph of agents tuvl lint project --strict 5 Tasks One task per model, step and example tuvl list tasks 6 Generate and lock Schemas, tests from the examples, the lock tuvl generate code , tuvl generate lock 7 The gate Seven checks that must all pass see below 8 Run The server, a real request, a real approval tuvl dev 9 Change A spec change flows through the checks tuvl show drift 10 Ship Dockerfile, Helm chart, image tuvl ship Who does what The coding agent builds; tuvl referees. In the agent track you write the intent and review the result, and the agent does stages 2 to 6 by running tuvl's commands until they are green. In the manual track you do those stages yourself. Every tab below shows both. Stages 7 to 10 are the same either way. Prefer to start from an idea? This guide writes the spec by hand. If you have a brief (Markdown, PDF or Word, or a web page, Jira issue or GitHub issue given with --url ) and a coding agent installed, tuvl import idea brief.pdf → tuvl generate spec → tuvl approve spec → tuvl generate tasks → tuvl generate code --spec … does stages 2 to 6 with your agent, one pull request per task, and the same gate at the end. See Authoring with a coding agent .
docs.title: The map

docs.text: tuvl init refunds -y --preset ollama cd refunds -y accepts every default. --preset writes llms/default.yaml for the provider you will use later ( gemini , openai , anthropic or ollama ); this project calls no model, so any preset works. Leave out --sample : that flag adds a ready-made triage example, and here you build your own. refunds/ ├── AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md rules for coding agents (CLAUDE.md just points at AGENTS.md) ├── .agents/skills/ 14 skills for coding agents (mirrored to .claude/skills/) ├── pyproject.toml your Python dependencies (uv) ├── .env, .env.example secrets and connection settings (.env is git-ignored) ├── .tuvl/ project identity (project.yaml) and system settings ├── datasources/postgres.yaml the database connection, read from .env ├── llms/default.yaml the model preset ├── models/ workflows/ agents/ artifacts/ federation/ empty, you fill them └── README.md With a coding agent init already gave the agent everything it needs: AGENTS.md holds the non-negotiable rules (never infer project state, never hand-edit generated files, finish every change green), and the skills in .agents/skills/ teach it each stage: tuvl-spec , tuvl-plan , tuvl-task-loop , one skill per engine ( agent-code , agent-tool , agent-llm , agent-loop , agent-decide , agent-human , agent-map ), tuvl-data , tuvl-test , tuvl-harden and tuvl-ship . Give the agent tuvl's own tools by adding the development MCP server to the agent's config: { "mcpServers": { "tuvl": { "command": "tuvl", "args": ["mcp", "-d", "."] } } } It offers validate , spec_check , spec_verify , spec_status , spec_diff , get_contract , list_agents , explain_error , codegen and test , all read-only. Add --allow-write to also allow codegen_write , run_workflow and pin_fixture . Without MCP the agent runs the same commands in a shell with --json . After you upgrade tuvl, tuvl update skills --diff shows what would change in the skills and tuvl update skills applies it. By hand Nothing more to set up. If you do not use a coding agent, tuvl init --no-ai-skills skips the .agents/ directory (the agent rules and skills).
docs.title: 1. Create the project

docs.text: The spec is the one document that says what the project is for. tuvl create spec writes a template that already passes the check: tuvl create spec refund-request A spec is Markdown. # Intent and # Policies are prose for people and the agent. Three parts are structured , and tuvl checks them: # Data (the models), # Flows (the steps, routes and ends) and the tuvl-example blocks under # Acceptance (each one becomes a test). The grammar is in Spec-driven development . With a coding agent You decide what ; the agent writes the structured parts with the tuvl-spec skill. Give it the intent in plain words and ask for the spec only: Use the tuvl-spec skill. Write specs/refund-request.md for this: customers request a refund on an order ( order_id , amount , reason ). If the amount is 100 or less, record it. If it is more, a finance lead (group finance_lead , 24 hours) must approve first; rejected or expired means no refund. An unknown order is a 404. Include an example for every end. Do not build anything yet. Run tuvl lint spec until it has no blocking findings, then show me. Review it before anything is built. This is the cheapest place to catch a wrong idea: Does every end have the right HTTP status, and an example ( tuvl lint spec warns with S011 if not)? Who is allowed to call the flow, and who may approve (S010, S013)? Is the threshold the one you meant, and is it in # Policies too? Is every model marked (new) or (existing) correctly? By hand Replace the template with the spec below. It is the whole project in one file. specs/refund-request.md --- name: refund-request owner: payments-team workflow: refund_request --- # Intent Customers ask for a refund on an order. A small refund is recorded straight away; a larger one waits for a finance lead, who approves or rejects it. # Data - **Order** (existing) — `id` (uuid), `total` (numeric; required) - **Refund** (new) — `order_id` (uuid → Order; required), `amount` (numeric; required), `reason` (text), `status` (enum: recorded | approved; required; default recorded) # Flows ## Flow: refund_request Trigger: POST /api/refunds · signed-in Input: `order_id` (uuid), `amount` (float), `reason` (str) Ends: default 201 · unknown_order 404 · rejected 200 · failed 500 - failed: no example — a create on a new row has no conflict to provoke 1. `load_order` — tool db read Order · in `order_id` · out `order` (Order) - not_found → END.unknown_order 2. `check_amount` — decide rules · in `amount` · out `lane` (enum[auto, review]) - `amount <= 100` → auto - otherwise → review - auto → `record_refund` - review → `finance_review` 3. `finance_review` — human group finance_lead · expires 24h · in `amount` · out `approved` (bool) - true → `record_refund` - false, expired → END.rejected 4. `record_refund` — tool db create Refund · in `order_id`, `amount`, `reason` · out `refund` (Refund) - conflict → END.failed # Policies A refund above 100 is never recorded without a finance lead's approval. # Acceptance ```tuvl-example name: a small refund is recorded given: { Order: [{ id: "6f1c0a52-2a8e-4d0b-9a77-0b9d7c2f1e10", total: 120 }] } input: { order_id: "6f1c0a52-2a8e-4d0b-9a77-0b9d7c2f1e10", amount: 40, reason: "Arrived broken." } expect: { end: default, path: [load_order, check_amount, record_refund] } ``` ```tuvl-example name: an unknown order is refused input: { order_id: "11111111-2222-4333-8444-555555555555", amount: 40, reason: "No such order." } expect: { end: unknown_order, path: [load_order] } ``` ```tuvl-example name: a large refund waits for a finance lead given: { Order: [{ id: "6f1c0a52-2a8e-4d0b-9a77-0b9d7c2f1e10", total: 900 }] } input: { order_id: "6f1c0a52-2a8e-4d0b-9a77-0b9d7c2f1e10", amount: 400, reason: "Wrong size." } expect: { end_or_wait: human, path_includes: [check_amount] } ``` ```tuvl-example name: a finance lead rejects a large refund given: { Order: [{ id: "6f1c0a52-2a8e-4d0b-9a77-0b9d7c2f1e10", total: 900 }] } input: { order_id: "6f1c0a52-2a8e-4d0b-9a77-0b9d7c2f1e10", amount: 400, reason: "Wrong size." } mocks: finance_review: { signal: "false", outputs: { approved: false } } expect: { end: rejected, path: [load_order, check_amount, finance_review] } ``` Reading the flow: each numbered line is a step ( id , engine, inputs in , outputs out ), and the indented lines are routes. tool db read Order loads the order and routes not_found to the end unknown_order . decide rules picks a lane from the amount. human group finance_lead waits for a person. tool db create Refund stores the result. failed: no example is a waiver: the spec says on purpose that this end has no example, and a reviewer can see why. Now check it. Nothing is built yet, so the spec is allowed to be ahead of the project: tuvl lint spec specs/refund-request.md ✗ S007 :11 Order is marked (existing) but is not in models/ · WAIVED :21 flow refund_request: end `failed` has no example — a create on a new row has no conflict to provoke ✗ is blocking and ! is a warning. S007 is the next thing to do: the spec says Order already exists, so tuvl expects models/order.yaml . Every finding names a line and a rule; the full list (S001 to S021) is in the spec reference .
docs.title: 2. Write the spec

docs.text: With a coding agent Ask for the models with the tuvl-data skill: "Create the models from # Data in the spec." It writes one ModelDefinition per model and runs tuvl lint spec until S007 is gone. By hand Order is an existing table that the flow only reads. Refund is new. kind: ModelDefinition version: v1 metadata: name: Order schema_version: v1 description: A customer order. Already in the database; the refund flow only reads it. spec: tablename: orders fields: - name: id type: uuid primary_key: true - name: total type: numeric required: true kind: ModelDefinition version: v1 metadata: name: Refund schema_version: v1 description: A refund recorded against an order. spec: tablename: refunds api: crud: [list, read] fields: - name: id type: uuid primary_key: true input: false - name: order_id type: uuid required: true - name: amount type: numeric required: true - name: reason type: text - name: status type: enum enum_values: [recorded, approved] default: recorded required: true - name: created_at type: timestamptz input: false A few things worth knowing: input: false keeps a server-generated field out of the create schema, enum_values plus default give the status its starting value, and api: crud: [list, read] exposes read-only routes for refunds (writes go through the workflow). The model YAML has no foreign-key option, so uuid → Order in the spec is checked against a plain uuid field. tuvl lint spec # S007 is gone
docs.title: 3. Data models

docs.text: A workflow is a graph of agents . Each agent has a typed contract ( inputs , outputs , the signals it can emit) and an engine that does the work. Routes connect signals to the next agent or to a named end, and there are no implicit edges. Agent Engine What it does load_order tool (db read) Loads the order; not_found ends as unknown_order (404) check_amount decide (rules) amount <= 100 is auto , anything else is review finance_review human Waits for a person in finance_lead ; false or expired ends as rejected record_refund tool (db create) Writes the refund; a conflict ends as failed With a coding agent The agent builds the workflow with the tuvl-task-loop skill, one task at a time, and picks the engine skill for each step ( agent-tool , agent-decide , agent-human ). The loop it follows is the same one you would: tuvl list tasks --json says which task is next and why others are blocked. Build what the task targets, exactly as the spec line says. tuvl generate code after any contract change. tuvl lint project --json and tuvl verify spec --json ; fix every error. tuvl run tests --json until a passing test goes through the step. Repeat until tuvl list tasks --strict exits 0. A step it cannot finish stays pending (a contract with no implementation) instead of being faked. Only a code agent needs Python, and then only the function body. Review the diff. Compare workflows/refund_request.yaml with the spec line by line. tuvl spec verify does the same comparison for you (stage 7), but a person should still read it once. By hand workflows/refund_request.yaml kind: Workflow version: tuvl/v2 metadata: name: refund_request description: Record a refund; a large one waits for a finance lead. spec: models: [Order, Refund] trigger: http: { path: /api/refunds, method: POST } input: order_id: uuid amount: float reason: str agents: - id: load_order description: Load the order being refunded engine: tool inputs: { order_id: uuid } outputs: { order: Order } tool: use: db model: Order op: read where: { id: "{{ order_id }}" } routes: default: check_amount not_found: END.unknown_order error: END.failed - id: check_amount description: A refund of 100 or less is recorded straight away; a larger one needs a lead engine: decide inputs: { amount: float } outputs: { lane: "enum[auto, review]" } decide: rules: - { when: "amount <= 100", then: auto } - { when: "true", then: review } routes: auto: record_refund review: finance_review error: END.failed - id: finance_review description: A finance lead approves or rejects a large refund engine: human inputs: { amount: float } outputs: { approved: bool } human: title: "Refund of {{ amount }}" instruction: Approve to record this refund. show: [amount] required_group: finance_lead expires: 24h route_on: approved routes: "true": record_refund "false": END.rejected expired: END.rejected error: END.failed - id: record_refund description: Record the refund engine: tool inputs: { order_id: uuid, amount: float, reason: str } outputs: { refund: Refund } tool: use: db model: Refund op: create values: order_id: "{{ order_id }}" amount: "{{ amount }}" reason: "{{ reason }}" routes: default: END conflict: END.failed error: END.failed outputs: default: status: 201 body: { id: "{{ refund.id }}", amount: "{{ refund.amount }}", status: "{{ refund.status }}" } unknown_order: status: 404 body: { error: no such order } rejected: status: 200 body: { status: rejected } failed: status: 500 body: { error: the refund could not be recorded } Points to notice: routes lists every signal an agent can emit. tuvl lint project rejects a missing route, so a path you forgot is an error, not a surprise at run time. decide rules are { when, then } , first match wins, and the last rule is when: "true" . human has required_group , an expires , and route_on: approved , which turns the boolean answer into the routes "true" and "false" (quoted, they are YAML strings). outputs maps each end to a status and a body. default is the success end. tuvl lint project --strict Models detected: 2 Order, Refund Code agents: none Errors: 0 Warnings: 0 refund_request 4 agents · 3 deterministic · 1 external · worst-case 0 tok needs models: none — no LLM or decision model required ✓ Validation passed — project looks good! The summary line is the determinism profile : three agents are deterministic, one waits for a person (external), and the worst-case token cost is 0 because no model is involved. When you add an llm step later, this line grows a token budget you set. A typo is caught here, not in production Writing a decide rule as - when: "amount <= 100" with value: auto (instead of then: auto ) fails with [V001] spec.agents[check_amount].decide.rules[0].then: Field required . Every error carries a code; tuvl lint project lists them all, and the agent's explain_error tool explains one.
docs.title: 4. The workflow

docs.text: The task list is how tuvl measures progress. It has one task per new model , per step and per example , plus a manual task for anything only a person can do (credentials for an HTTP or MCP step). tuvl never plans with a model, and it never lets anyone set a status: a task's status is derived from the project. Status Means todo Not built yet (a pending agent, a missing file, an example with no test) in_progress Built, but lint project or verify spec reports a problem implemented Validates cleanly and matches the spec tested A passing test covers it done Nothing blocks shipping With a coding agent The agent writes specs/refund-request.tasks.yaml with the tuvl-plan skill, after the spec has no blocking findings. Check its work: every model, step and example should have a task, and no task carries an estimate or a hand-set status (P004). By hand The only values you cannot invent are the hashes . They tie a task to the exact version of the spec section it came from, and tuvl prints them: tuvl lint spec --json | jq -r '.specs[0].hash' # the spec's hash tuvl lint spec --json | jq -r '.specs[0].sections[] | "\(.anchor) \(.hash)"' intent 7ac196eddd46 data 38fe48d961df flows 7d14b7826850 flow-refund-request d4288ac72c9b policies 45985c2e44d8 acceptance d955f6a357cf Put the spec hash in metadata.spec_hash , and each task's section anchor and hash in its spec_ref . The file has nine tasks: the Refund model ( Order is existing, so it needs no task), the four steps and the four examples. specs/refund-request.tasks.yaml kind: TaskPlan version: tuvl/v2 metadata: { name: refund-request, spec: specs/refund-request.md, spec_hash: f010f2617b63 } spec: tasks: - id: T1 title: Refund model type: model spec_ref: { anchor: data, hash: 38fe48d961df } target: { model: Refund } - id: T2 title: Load the order (tool db read) type: agent spec_ref: { anchor: flow-refund-request, hash: d4288ac72c9b } target: { workflow: refund_request, agent: load_order } depends_on: [T1] - id: T3 title: Route by amount (decide rules) type: agent spec_ref: { anchor: flow-refund-request, hash: d4288ac72c9b } target: { workflow: refund_request, agent: check_amount } depends_on: [T2] - id: T4 title: Finance lead review (human) type: agent spec_ref: { anchor: flow-refund-request, hash: d4288ac72c9b } target: { workflow: refund_request, agent: finance_review } depends_on: [T3] - id: T5 title: Record the refund (tool db create) type: agent spec_ref: { anchor: flow-refund-request, hash: d4288ac72c9b } target: { workflow: refund_request, agent: record_refund } depends_on: [T1, T3, T4] - id: T6 title: "Example: a small refund is recorded" type: test spec_ref: { anchor: acceptance, hash: d955f6a357cf } target: { workflow: refund_request, example: a small refund is recorded } depends_on: [T5] - id: T7 title: "Example: an unknown order is refused" type: test spec_ref: { anchor: acceptance, hash: d955f6a357cf } target: { workflow: refund_request, example: an unknown order is refused } depends_on: [T2] - id: T8 title: "Example: a large refund waits for a finance lead" type: test spec_ref: { anchor: acceptance, hash: d955f6a357cf } target: { workflow: refund_request, example: a large refund waits for a finance lead } depends_on: [T4] - id: T9 title: "Example: a finance lead rejects a large refund" type: test spec_ref: { anchor: acceptance, hash: d955f6a357cf } target: { workflow: refund_request, example: a finance lead rejects a large refund } depends_on: [T4] depends_on orders the work (the model before the steps that use it, an example after the steps it runs through). The hashes come from the exact text of the spec: if you type the spec above unchanged, the task list passes as printed, and any edit to a section changes its hash (and is reported as P005 until you refresh it, as in stage 9 ). Look at the board: tuvl list tasks Before the tests exist it shows exactly what is missing and why, for example: T1 implemented Refund model tuvl.lock is missing T2 implemented blocked Load the order (tool db read) no passing Test covers refund_request.load_order waiting on T1 T6 todo blocked Example: a small refund is recorded no generated test for example 'a small refund is recorded' — run tuvl generate code waiting on T5 The reasons are the to-do list. The next stage clears them.
docs.title: 5. The task list

docs.text: tuvl generate code tuvl generate lock + agents/_generated/schemas.py + tests/refund_request/a-small-refund-is-recorded.yaml + tests/refund_request/an-unknown-order-is-refused.yaml + tests/refund_request/a-large-refund-waits-for-a-finance-lead.yaml + tests/refund_request/a-finance-lead-rejects-a-large-refund.yaml 5 file(s) written. wrote tuvl.lock: 0 model(s), 0 artifact(s), 0 judge(s), 0 MCP tool(s) tuvl generate code writes what follows mechanically from your YAML and spec: typed schemas for every agent ( agents/_generated/schemas.py ), and one test per tuvl-example in the spec. It never writes a function body. If the project had a code agent it would also write its stub and keep your code on every later run ( Code generation ). Never edit generated files; change the spec and run it again. tuvl generate lock writes tuvl.lock : the tuvl version and, when you have them, the exact model ids, prompt hashes and MCP tool schemas the project depends on. It is empty of those here, and it still matters: tuvl ship refuses a stale lock (V024), so a model upgrade can never reach production by accident. Commit it.
docs.title: 6. Generate and lock

docs.text: Seven commands decide whether the project is consistent. Run them together; this is also your CI: tuvl lint spec && tuvl lint project --strict && tuvl generate code --check && tuvl verify lock \ && tuvl run tests --strict && tuvl verify spec --strict && tuvl list tasks --strict Command It proves tuvl lint spec The spec is complete and consistent (S001 to S016) and the task list matches it (P001 to P005) tuvl lint project --strict The workflows are well-formed: routes, types, data flow, policy (V001 to V036). --strict makes warnings fail tuvl generate code --check Generated files are up to date; exits 1 if anything would change tuvl verify lock tuvl.lock matches the project tuvl run tests --strict The tests pass; --strict also fails a result that only passed through unimplemented steps tuvl verify spec --strict The workflow matches the spec step by step (R001 to R010) tuvl list tasks --strict Every task is done $ tuvl run tests --strict PASS a-finance-lead-rejects-a-large-refund (refund_request → END.rejected, 0 tok) PASS a-large-refund-waits-for-a-finance-lead (refund_request → END.?, 0 tok) PASS a-small-refund-is-recorded (refund_request → END.default, 0 tok) PASS an-unknown-order-is-refused (refund_request → END.unknown_order, 0 tok) 4 passed · 0 stubbed (not counted) · 0 failed $ tuvl verify spec --strict refund_request load_order tool db read Order :23 ✓ 4 passed check_amount decide rules :25 ✓ 3 passed finance_review human group finance_lead :30 ✓ mocked in 1 record_refund tool db create Refund :33 ✓ 1 passed 0 mismatch(es) · steps implemented 4/4 · exercised by real tests 3/4 $ tuvl list tasks --strict T1 done Refund model ... T9 done Example: a finance lead rejects a large refund tests 4/4 passing · tuvl.lock current Two details are worth understanding: Tests run offline against an in-memory database. They mock only what is non-deterministic, external or human. Here that is the finance_review step, because nobody answers a form in a test. Business logic ( tool db , decide rules, code ) runs for real, and the order is seeded with given: in the example. That is why verify spec says 3/4 are exercised by real tests: the fourth is mocked on purpose. A mock cannot hide a gap. If a step is still pending , a test that passes through it is reported STUBBED , does not count, and fails --strict . With a coding agent The agent runs this gate after every change and does not stop until it is green. Run it yourself once at the end; that is your acceptance test of the agent's work. By hand If a command fails, its output names the rule and the line. Fix that, and rerun the gate. The troubleshooting table lists the messages you are most likely to meet.
docs.title: 7. The gate

docs.text: So far nothing needed a database. To call the workflow you need PostgreSQL. Create a database and point .env at it: createdb refunds POSTGRES_HOST=localhost POSTGRES_PORT=5432 POSTGRES_DB=refunds POSTGRES_USER=postgres POSTGRES_PASSWORD=... Start the engine in dev mode: tuvl dev --show-key It prints a security key and the address of Insight, the browser UI ( http://localhost:8885/insight/ ). In dev mode the key works as an admin bearer token. Insight shows the workflow as a graph, runs it with Run , and lists approvals under Runs . On startup tuvl creates the tables for your models; the Order table stands in for the one your system already has, so add an order to refund: export KEY=<the security key> psql refunds -c "insert into orders (id, total) values ('6f1c0a52-2a8e-4d0b-9a77-0b9d7c2f1e10', 900)" A small refund is recorded at once: curl -s -X POST localhost:8885/api/refunds \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $KEY" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{"order_id":"6f1c0a52-2a8e-4d0b-9a77-0b9d7c2f1e10","amount":40,"reason":"Arrived broken."}' HTTP 201 {"id":"7150932f-1f44-4826-af70-d4d5dcef22b4","amount":40.0,"status":"recorded"} An unknown order takes the unknown_order end: HTTP 404 {"error":"no such order"} A large refund ( "amount":400 ) stops at finance_review . The response is 202 with a run descriptor instead of a refund: HTTP 202 {"run_id":"97b2631a-…","workflow":"refund_request","status":"waiting_human", "current_agent":"finance_review","tokens_used":0, "approval":{"approval_id":"7a1939d5-…","kind":"human","required_group":"finance_lead", "title":"Refund of 400.0","form":{"approved":{"type":"bool","required":true}}}, ...} The run is parked in the database, so it survives a restart. Now approve it. Try with the same key: curl -s -X POST localhost:8885/api/approvals/$APPROVAL_ID \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $KEY" -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"values":{"approved":true}}' HTTP 403 {"detail":"the principal who triggered this run cannot approve it"} That is a deliberate rule: nobody approves their own run . The approver is a different user who holds the approvals:decide scope in the step's group. Create that person (this is also what the IAM page in Insight does). The first administrator comes from POST /auth/bootstrap , which works only while there are no users: B=localhost:8885 curl -s -X POST $B/auth/bootstrap -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{"email":"admin@example.com","password":"<a strong password>","first_name":"Ada","last_name":"Admin"}' AT=$(curl -s -X POST $B/auth/token -d "username=admin@example.com&password=<a strong password>" | jq -r .access_token) A=(-H "Authorization: Bearer $AT" -H "Content-Type: application/json") ROLE=$(curl -s -X POST $B/auth/admin/roles "${A[@]}" \ -d '{"name":"finance_lead","scopes":["approvals:decide","runs:read"]}' | jq -r .id) USER=$(curl -s -X POST $B/auth/admin/users "${A[@]}" \ -d '{"email":"lead@example.com","password":"<another password>","first_name":"Lee","last_name":"Lead"}' | jq -r .id) curl -s -X POST $B/auth/admin/users/$USER/roles/$ROLE "${A[@]}" # 204 Role names become the token's groups , which is how required_group: finance_lead finds them. Now the lead signs in, sees the approval and decides: LT=$(curl -s -X POST $B/auth/token -d "username=lead@example.com&password=<another password>" | jq -r .access_token) L=(-H "Authorization: Bearer $LT" -H "Content-Type: application/json") curl -sL $B/api/approvals/ "${L[@]}" # the lead's inbox curl -s -X POST $B/api/approvals/$APPROVAL_ID "${L[@]}" -d '{"values":{"approved":true}}' The run continues from where it stopped and finishes on the default end: curl -s $B/api/runs/$RUN_ID -H "Authorization: Bearer $KEY" | jq -c '{status, end, output}' {"status":"completed","end":"default","output":{"body":{"id":"3ad7dbf2-…","amount":400.0,"status":"recorded"},"status":201}} TUVL_URL=http://localhost:8885 TUVL_TOKEN=$KEY tuvl list runs # every run, with its end tuvl follow run <run_id> # follows a run until it ends (Ctrl-C to stop) Every step of every run is journaled, so you can see what happened and replay it. Open Insight ( http://localhost:8885/insight/ ) to look at the same project: Specs is the task board from stage 5: nine tasks, all in Done . Workflows → refund_request draws the graph ( load_order , check_amount , the orange finance_review and record_refund , and the four ends) and repeats the profile: 4 agents · 3 deterministic · 1 external · worst-case 0 tok . Runs lists every run. Open the parked one to see the approval form and the journal: load_order → default , check_amount decided review by rule#2 , finance_review approval requested . Submitting the form as the user who started the run shows the same refusal as the API. After the lead decides, the journal adds approval decided by … , resumed and run completed END.default (201) with the response, and Pin as fixture turns the run into a test that replays with zero tokens. The parked run is a row in your database, so it also survives restarting the engine: stop tuvl dev , start it again, and the run is still waiting_human . Dev keys are for development In production there is no session key: callers use signed tokens, and trigger.http.public: true is the only way to open a route without one. See Authentication .
docs.title: 8. Run it

docs.text: The spec stays the source of truth. Suppose finance raises the automatic limit from 100 to 200. Change the spec first (the flow's rule and the policy), and let tuvl show you what moved: tuvl lint spec ! P005 specs/refund-request.tasks.yaml:11 T2: spec section #flow-refund-request changed since the task was written ! P005 specs/refund-request.tasks.yaml:17 T3: ... 0 blocking · 4 warning(s) tuvl verify spec check_amount decide rules :25 ✗ mismatch 3 passed ✗ R007 :25 `check_amount`: the workflow's rules differ from the spec's tuvl show drift lists the stale tasks and the spec sections no task covers. Now the work is clear: the workflow still says 100, and four tasks point at a section that changed. With a coding agent Say it in terms of the spec, and let the agent follow the loop: Finance raised the automatic limit from 100 to 200. Update the spec (the flow rule and the policy) and add an example for a refund of 150. Then bring the task list and the workflow back in line and run the full gate. Do not change the workflow before the spec. The tuvl-plan skill tells it to refresh the spec_ref hashes it has reviewed, to add tasks for new steps and to mark removed ones obsolete: true rather than delete them. By hand Change the rule in workflows/refund_request.yaml to amount <= 200 , then refresh the hashes in the task list from tuvl lint spec --json (the same commands as stage 5), and rerun the gate: tuvl lint spec && tuvl verify spec --strict && tuvl run tests --strict && tuvl list tasks --strict All four commands exit 0 again. The order matters: spec first, then the workflow . If you change the workflow first, verify spec reports a contradiction until the spec catches up.
docs.title: 9. Change it later

docs.text: When the gate is green, shipping is one command. In CI, run the gate on every pull request (this is the exact gate the example projects use): name: CI gate on: [push, pull_request] jobs: gate: runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: - uses: actions/checkout@v4 - uses: astral-sh/setup-uv@v5 - name: Install tuvl run: uv tool install --python 3.13 "tuvl[standard]>=2.0.0,<3" - name: Gate run: | tuvl lint spec tuvl lint project --strict tuvl generate code --check tuvl verify lock --no-mcp tuvl run tests --strict tuvl verify spec --strict tuvl list tasks --strict Then: tuvl generate key --write # a persistent signing key for production tokens tuvl ship -t registry.example.com/refunds:1.0 # add --push to push, --no-build to skip docker Step 1/3 — validate ✓ Validation passed ✓ tuvl.lock is current (tuvl 2.0.0) ✓ tuvl extras: none — the base install is enough not installed: mcp, redis, vector, otel-grpc Step 2/3 — deploy artifacts wrote deploy/Dockerfile wrote .dockerignore wrote deploy/chart/refunds/Chart.yaml ... image contents: 16 file(s) — agents/ 2, models/ 3, workflows/ 2, tuvl.lock, ... Step 3/3 — container image tuvl ship runs the same validation first, so nothing ships that does not validate: no pending agents (V010), a current lock (V024), no development files in the image (V027). It then writes: deploy/Dockerfile , pinned to the tuvl version in tuvl.lock , installing only the extras your project uses. This one needs none, so the image carries the bare install (about 65 MB of Python packages). A .dockerignore that is an allowlist : only the project's models, workflows, agents, datasources, tuvl.lock and runtime config enter the image. Specs, tests, task lists, .env and the agent skills stay out. A Helm chart in deploy/chart/refunds/ , with an optional split into API and worker pods. Deploy it with the tools you already have: kubectl create secret generic refunds-env --from-env-file=.env helm install refunds deploy/chart/refunds --set image.repository=registry.example.com/refunds # separate API and worker pods: helm upgrade refunds deploy/chart/refunds --set split=true --set worker.replicaCount=3 The secret must hold TUVL_SIGNING_KEY (from tuvl generate key ), POSTGRES_PASSWORD , and the variable of every model the workflows use (none here). A production engine refuses to start while one is missing. The container runs in production mode: no dev routes, no Insight, JSON logs. The chart does not include Postgres, so point POSTGRES_HOST at yours. More: Shipping to production . tuvl deploy is coming A hosted, managed tuvl engine that runs your backend services is planned, so there is no image or cluster to operate. tuvl deploy is the command for it. It is not available yet: today it prints a message, deploys nothing and exits 1. Until then, tuvl ship plus helm is the way.
docs.title: 10. Ship it

docs.text: Every project already carries an identity file, .tuvl/project.yaml , with a stable id and your git name and email. If you want the project listed in the public catalogue at nest.tuvl.io, look first: tuvl show project tuvl set project description "Refund approvals: small refunds at once, large ones wait for a lead." tuvl register project # prints the exact payload and asks; answer n to only look Registering is public and is tied to the GitHub account you sign in with. The author name in the listing is your git name , so check it first ( tuvl set project author "…" ). Your email stays private unless you add --public-email , and nothing about your workflows, models or data is sent. If you use a coding agent, it will not register on its own: it only does so when you ask. Details, every field and the error messages: Project and Catalogue .

docs.text: I want to Run Start a project tuvl init <name> -y --preset <provider> Start a spec tuvl create spec <name> (or tuvl import idea <brief> then tuvl generate spec ) Approve a spec / derive its tasks tuvl approve spec <spec> / tuvl generate tasks <spec> Build the tasks with your coding agent tuvl generate code --spec <spec> --all Review the agents' Python tuvl review code ( --agent for a second opinion) See what was done to the project tuvl show audit (or Insight → Audit) Check the spec / the build against it tuvl lint spec / tuvl verify spec See what to do next tuvl list tasks ( --json for agents) See what changed since the plan tuvl show drift Generate schemas, stubs, tests tuvl generate code ( --check in CI) Check the workflows tuvl lint project --strict Run the tests tuvl run tests --strict Pin models and tools tuvl generate lock ( --check in CI) Run it locally tuvl dev --show-key Look at runs tuvl list runs , tuvl follow run <id> Serve it to a coding agent tuvl serve mcp Package it tuvl ship -t <image> ( --format archive for a zip/tar you run with uv ) Look at, edit or publish the project's identity tuvl show project , tuvl set project , tuvl register project

docs.text: Installation ¶ This guide walks you through installing tuvl and its dependencies. Prerequisites ¶ Before installing tuvl, ensure you have: Python 3.13 or 3.14 — tuvl 2.0 supports >=3.13,<3.15 . uv picks a compatible interpreter automatically. uv — Fast Python package manager (recommended) PostgreSQL — For data persistence (optional for development) Docker — Optional. The easiest way to run PostgreSQL, Redis and Laya locally, and required by tuvl ship to build the production image Redis — Optional for tuvl dev ; needed when you run more than one worker ( why ) Laya ( tuvl/laya-serve ) — Optional. A self-hosted decision model for decide agents; runs as its own container Ollama — For local LLM inference (optional) What you actually need To try tuvl you need Python and uv, and a PostgreSQL database. Everything else above is opt-in: Redis only matters for multi-worker deployments, and Laya only if a decide agent uses it as its decision model. Python 3.14 tuvl 1.x was held to Python 3.13 because its token library ( biscuit-python ) had no 3.14 builds. tuvl 2.0 signs tokens as standard JWTs and runs on 3.13 and 3.14 on Linux, macOS and Windows. Installing uv ¶ macOS / Linux curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh Windows powershell -c "irm https://astral.sh/uv/install.ps1 | iex" pip pip install uv Upgrading from 1.x ¶ uv tool install tuvl installs tuvl 2.0.0. There is no 1.x compatibility layer: a 1.x workflow fails to load with an error pointing at the 2.0 format (see what's new ). To move an existing install, run uv tool upgrade tuvl . The TypeScript client is npm install @tuvl/client . Installing tuvl CLI ¶ Install the tuvl CLI globally using uv: # Base CLI only uv tool install tuvl # With dev server and built-in UI (recommended) uv tool install "tuvl[standard]" Tip tuvl[standard] includes the dev server ( tuvl dev ), the built-in tuvl insight UI, hot-reload support, the development tools ( tuvl generate code , tuvl run tests , tuvl serve mcp ) and every extra below. The base install is the production server and is about 65 MB installed. tuvl ship builds production images from it and adds only the extras your project uses. Verify the installation: tuvl --version Installing tuvl as a Project Dependency ¶ For projects that embed the engine directly: # Base engine uv add tuvl # With dev server and built-in UI uv add "tuvl[standard]" Or with pip: pip install "tuvl[standard]" Extras ¶ The base tuvl has no package for a feature you may not use. Install the extra when you use the feature: Extra Adds You need it for tuvl[mcp] mcp use: mcp tools, a loop calling an MCP server, exporting a workflow as an MCP tool, tuvl serve mcp tuvl[redis] redis a type: redis datasource tuvl[vector] pgvector collections, embeddings and tuvl.data_search / tuvl.data_ingest tuvl[otel-grpc] OTLP gRPC exporter TUVL_OTLP_PROTOCOL=grpc (HTTP/protobuf is the default and needs nothing) tuvl[codegen] libcst tuvl generate code and tuvl init --sample tuvl[test] aiosqlite tuvl run tests tuvl[review] ruff tuvl review code tuvl[pdf] pypdf tuvl import idea of PDF ideas (Word and Markdown need nothing extra) tuvl[tui] textual the terminal UI that tuvl dev starts on a terminal uv add "tuvl[mcp,redis]" Using a feature without its extra fails with the command to run, for example pip install 'tuvl[mcp]' . You do not choose extras for production by hand: tuvl ship reads the project and installs exactly the ones it needs. Model providers and blob storage (S3, Azure, GCS, local disk) are built in and need no extra. Optional Dependencies ¶ PostgreSQL ¶ macOS (Homebrew) brew install postgresql@16 brew services start postgresql@16 Ubuntu/Debian sudo apt update sudo apt install postgresql postgresql-contrib sudo systemctl start postgresql Docker docker run -d \ --name tuvl-postgres \ -e POSTGRES_USER=postgres \ -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=postgres \ -e POSTGRES_DB=tuvl \ -p 5432:5432 \ postgres:16-alpine Redis (optional) ¶ Redis shares OAuth state and the token-revocation list between workers. A single tuvl dev process works without it (an in-process fallback is used); add it before running more than one worker. Install tuvl[redis] to use it. See Redis configuration for the datasource file. macOS (Homebrew) brew install redis brew services start redis Ubuntu/Debian sudo apt install redis-server sudo systemctl start redis-server Docker docker run -d --name tuvl-redis -p 6379:6379 redis:7-alpine Then add datasources/redis-primary.yaml with type: redis , host: ${REDIS_HOST:localhost} . Laya decision server (optional) ¶ Laya is an open-weight model that picks one value of a decide agent's enum with a confidence. It runs on CPU in its own container, offline, with verified weights baked in. Use it when you want decisions made on your own infrastructure instead of calling a hosted model. The quickest route is to let tuvl init scaffold it: tuvl init my-project --decision-model laya -y cd my-project docker compose up -d laya # serves on http://localhost:8000 This writes llms/laya.yaml (a provider: laya AgentModel), LAYA_API_* entries in .env and a compose.yaml . To run the container by hand: English only (smaller) docker run -d --name laya -p 127.0.0.1:8000:8000 tuvl/laya-serve:0.4.7-1-en English + multilingual docker run -d --name laya -p 127.0.0.1:8000:8000 tuvl/laya-serve:0.4.7-1 Image Use with Memory …-en model: english about 2 GiB full model: auto or multilingual about 3.5 GiB The image is about 2.7 GB (CPU PyTorch plus the weights), amd64 and arm64. Check it is up with curl localhost:8000/health . Details, checkpoints and settings are in AI Models → Laya and Decide . Ollama (Local LLM) ¶ macOS brew install ollama ollama serve # In another terminal, pull a model ollama pull llama3 Linux curl -fsSL https://ollama.com/install.sh | sh ollama serve # In another terminal ollama pull llama3 Docker docker run -d \ --name ollama \ -p 11434:11434 \ -v ollama:/root/.ollama \ ollama/ollama docker exec ollama ollama pull llama3 Verifying Installation ¶ Create the sample project and run its checks: tuvl init my-project --sample --preset gemini -y # or openai | anthropic | ollama cd my-project tuvl lint project --strict tuvl run tests tuvl dev --auto-login tuvl dev serves the engine on port 8885 and Insight at http://127.0.0.1:8885/insight/ . With --auto-login this machine skips the key screen; otherwise paste the session key, stored in .tuvl/.dev-session ( tuvl dev --show-key prints it). Troubleshooting ¶ Windows: port already in use or permission denied ¶ Symptom — tuvl dev fails to start the engine on its default port ( 8885 ) with one of: [Errno 48] Address already in use / Only one usage of each socket address … is normally permitted PermissionError: [WinError 10013] An attempt was made to access a socket in a way forbidden by its access permissions Why this happens — either another process is already bound to the port, or — common on Windows — the port falls inside a range Windows has reserved for dynamic allocation. Hyper-V, WSL 2, and Docker Desktop routinely reserve large TCP ranges; binding a port inside a reserved range fails with WinError 10013 even though nothing is actively listening on it. Inspect the reserved ranges: netsh interface ipv4 show excludedportrange protocol=tcp If 8885 sits inside an excluded range (or is otherwise taken), run tuvl on a free port: One-off flag tuvl dev --port 8899 Environment variable # Persist a different port for all tuvl commands in this shell $env:TUVL_DEV_PORT = "8899" tuvl dev Tip The port also appears in the login URL tuvl prints ( http://127.0.0.1:<port>/insight/ ). If you rely on the OAuth callback flow, align TUVL_OAUTH_BASE_URL with the port you chose (defaults to http://localhost:8885 ). The default 8885 spells T·U·V·L on a phone keypad and deliberately avoids the crowded 8000 / 8080 / 8888 range — but any free, non-reserved port works. Next Steps ¶ Quickstart Guide — Build your first workflow Code generation — tuvl generate code : typed schemas, stubs and tests Shipping to production — tuvl ship : image, Helm chart, Laya and secrets Project Structure — Understand the project layout Agentic Manual — how tuvl projects are written

docs.text: Symptom — tuvl dev fails to start the engine on its default port ( 8885 ) with one of: [Errno 48] Address already in use / Only one usage of each socket address … is normally permitted PermissionError: [WinError 10013] An attempt was made to access a socket in a way forbidden by its access permissions Why this happens — either another process is already bound to the port, or — common on Windows — the port falls inside a range Windows has reserved for dynamic allocation. Hyper-V, WSL 2, and Docker Desktop routinely reserve large TCP ranges; binding a port inside a reserved range fails with WinError 10013 even though nothing is actively listening on it. Inspect the reserved ranges: netsh interface ipv4 show excludedportrange protocol=tcp If 8885 sits inside an excluded range (or is otherwise taken), run tuvl on a free port: One-off flag tuvl dev --port 8899 Environment variable # Persist a different port for all tuvl commands in this shell $env:TUVL_DEV_PORT = "8899" tuvl dev Tip The port also appears in the login URL tuvl prints ( http://127.0.0.1:<port>/insight/ ). If you rely on the OAuth callback flow, align TUVL_OAUTH_BASE_URL with the port you chose (defaults to http://localhost:8885 ). The default 8885 spells T·U·V·L on a phone keypad and deliberately avoids the crowded 8000 / 8080 / 8888 range — but any free, non-reserved port works.

docs.text: Quickstart ¶ This walks through the sample project: a support-ticket triage workflow with a spec, a task list, tests and a lock that pass the CI gate as created. Install tuvl as shown in Installation first. 1. Create the project ¶ tuvl init triage --sample --preset gemini -y # or openai | anthropic | ollama cd triage The preset writes llms/default.yaml (the agents' model) and reads the API key from your environment into .env . Point .env at a PostgreSQL database ( POSTGRES_* ). 2. Check it ¶ tuvl lint project --strict triage_ticket 4 agents · 2 deterministic · 1 bounded · 1 external · worst-case 500 tok ✓ Validation passed Every workflow gets a determinism profile and a worst-case token cost . Then run the tests — offline, with recorded and mocked results: tuvl run tests tuvl list tasks # every task derived as done 3. Open Insight ¶ tuvl dev --auto-login # http://localhost:8885/insight Workflows → triage_ticket shows the graph: classify (llm) → prioritise → review (human) → store (tool). Click a card to see its contract and engine. ▶ Run with a ticket. An urgent one stops at review : the Runs page shows the approval form; approve it and the run continues to store . 📌 Pin as fixture turns the run into a test that replays with zero tokens. 4. Call it ¶ curl -X POST localhost:8885/api/tickets/triage \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{"subject": "Refund", "body": "I was charged twice", "customer_email": "a@example.com"}' The response is the end's body ( 201 with the stored ticket), or 202 with a run descriptor when the run waits for a person. Follow it with tuvl follow run <run_id> or GET /api/runs/<run_id>/events (SSE). In dev mode the session key works as an admin token. 5. Change something ¶ Open specs/triage-ticket.md and add a policy. Then hand it to your coding agent (it has the tuvl-spec , tuvl-plan and tuvl-task-loop skills); tuvl referees the result: tuvl lint spec # the spec is well-formed tuvl show drift # what changed since the task list was written tuvl list tasks # the tasks, with status derived from the project The agent updates specs/triage-ticket.tasks.yaml and implements the tasks (YAML engine blocks; Python only for code agents). Then run the CI gate: tuvl lint spec && tuvl lint project --strict && tuvl generate code --check && tuvl verify lock \ && tuvl run tests --strict && tuvl verify spec --strict && tuvl list tasks --strict Next: the step-by-step guide from init to ship builds a project of your own, with a coding agent or by hand. Then the Agentic Manual and spec-driven development .

docs.text: Shipping to production ¶ tuvl ship turns a project into a container image and a Helm chart, or into a runnable archive. It is the same gate as CI: nothing ships that does not validate. tuvl generate key --write # a persistent signing key (TUVL_SIGNING_KEY) tuvl ship -t registry.example.com/triage:1.0.0 --push Image, archive, or both ¶ --format image (the default) builds the container image, labelled with a hash of the files the runtime uses and the commit. --format archive writes a reproducible tar.gz (or zip with --archive-format zip ) with run.sh , RUN.md , .env.example and BUILD-INFO.json , which you run with uv on a host without Docker. --format both does both; --no-image skips the image build. --out sets where files go. Before either, ship runs the deterministic spec gate: every spec under approval is approved and unchanged, lint spec and verify spec are clean, tasks are done ( --allow-incomplete to override), generated files are current, the agents' Python has no review errors, uv.lock is current and the tree is clean ( --allow-dirty ). What it does ¶ Gate. Runs the validation ( --strict also fails on warnings). A workflow with a pending agent (V010) is an error at ship time, and the project's tuvl.lock must be current. Deploy artifacts. Writes deploy/Dockerfile (pinned to the locked tuvl version), .dockerignore and a chart in deploy/chart/<name>/ . Existing files are kept unless you pass --force . Image. Runs docker build , and docker push with --push . The .dockerignore is an allowlist : only models, workflows, agents, artifacts, datasources, llms, federation, config, the lock and .tuvl/system.yaml / telemetry.yaml enter the image. Specs, task lists, tests, agent rules and skills, compose files and .env stay out; a development file in the image is refused (V027). The container runs in production mode: no dev routes, no Insight UI, JSON logs, telemetry on. Only what the project uses ¶ The image holds tuvl plus the extras your project needs and nothing else. tuvl ship decides from files, before the build, so the same project always produces the same image: Extra Installed when mcp a use: mcp tool, a loop MCP server, or a workflow with trigger.mcp.enabled redis a kind: DataSource with type: redis , or an agent imports redis vector a Collection or Embedding document, tuvl.data_search / tuvl.data_ingest , or an agent imports pgvector otel-grpc .tuvl/telemetry.yaml sets otlp_protocol: grpc generate code and run tests are development tools and never enter an image. Blob storage and every model provider are part of tuvl and add nothing. A project with none of the triggers above ships the bare install, about 65 MB of Python packages instead of the 320 MB of 2.0.0b4. ✓ tuvl extras: mcp mcp: workflows/triage.yaml: agent lookup calls an MCP server not installed: redis, vector, otel-grpc Your own packages. tuvl ship reads the imports in agents/*.py . A package that pyproject.toml does not declare stops the ship, because the container would fail mid-run; uv add it. Declared packages that no agent imports are listed and kept; remove them from pyproject.toml to slim the image. What the image carries. The chosen extras are written into deploy/Dockerfile as tuvl[...]==<locked version> and recorded as the image label io.tuvl.extras : docker inspect --format '{{ index .Config.Labels "io.tuvl.extras" }}' <image> . Something the scan cannot see. --extra mcp (or redis , vector , otel-grpc ) adds an extra, for example for a feature an environment variable turns on. A kept Dockerfile. Generated files are kept unless you pass --force . If a kept deploy/Dockerfile lacks an extra the project now needs, the ship stops and says so. Options ¶ Option Meaning -t , --tag Image reference. Defaults to <project>:<version> --no-build Write the Dockerfile and chart, skip docker build --push Push the image after a successful build --force Overwrite existing generated files --strict Treat validation warnings as errors --extra NAME Also install a tuvl extra ( mcp , redis , vector , otel-grpc ). Repeatable --with-laya / --without-laya Include the Laya decision server in the chart. Default: on when an AgentModel uses provider: laya Deploy ¶ kubectl create secret generic triage-env --from-env-file=.env helm install triage deploy/chart/triage --set image.repository=registry.example.com/triage The secret must hold TUVL_SIGNING_KEY , POSTGRES_PASSWORD and the variables of every model the workflows use. A production engine refuses to start while one is missing. For separate API and worker pods: helm install triage deploy/chart/triage --set split=true --set worker.replicaCount=3 Laya in the chart ¶ When a model uses provider: laya (or with --with-laya ), the chart gains a Laya Deployment and Service, and the engine's LAYA_API_BASE points at it. laya.enabled in values.yaml switches it. model: english auto / multilingual Image docker.io/tuvl/laya-serve:<version>-en docker.io/tuvl/laya-serve:<version> Memory request / limit 2 Gi / 3 Gi 4 Gi / 5 Gi tuvl ship chooses the image and memory from your models. Set LAYA_API_KEY in the secret to require a bearer key on the server. Leave Laya out with --without-laya (or --set laya.enabled=false ) when you use a hosted model instead. Redis ¶ The chart does not include Redis. Run more than one worker ( split=true , or several replicas) and you need one: point a type: redis datasource at it with REDIS_HOST , REDIS_PORT and REDIS_PASSWORD . See Redis configuration . Storage in the chart ¶ A kind: Storage store on local disk gets a persistent volume and fsGroup in the chart. Cloud stores (S3, Azure, GCS) need no volume, only their credentials in the secret. storage/ is on the image allowlist; a project shipped before storage existed needs tuvl ship --force once. See Blob Storage . Coming: tuvl deploy (managed hosting) ¶ tuvl deploy is planned as a hosted, managed tuvl engine that runs your backend services, so there is no image or cluster to operate. It is not available yet. Today the command only says so, deploys nothing and exits with status 1, so a script cannot mistake it for a deployment: $ tuvl deploy ╭─ tuvl deploy ───────────────────────────────────────────╮ │ Managed hosting is coming soon. │ │ It is not available yet, and nothing was deployed. │ │ Until then, build and deploy it yourself: tuvl ship │ ╰─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╯ Until it launches, you deploy the chart that tuvl ship writes with helm , as above. See also ¶ CLI reference Blob Storage AI Models Installation

docs.text: AI Models ¶ The AI Models section configures your AgentModel definitions — the model connections behind llm , loop and decide agents, judges and spec analysis. tuvl calls models with its own built-in client, so OpenAI, Anthropic, Gemini, Azure OpenAI, Bedrock, Vertex AI, Cohere, Ollama and any OpenAI-compatible endpoint connect with a single config file. See Models and Providers . File list ¶ The sidebar lists every file in your project's llms/ directory. Click any file to open the model editor. Form editor ¶ The form is split into three sections: Identity ¶ Field Description Name Snake-case identifier used to reference this model in workflow YAML (e.g. default ) Description Human-readable label shown in the portal Enabled Toggle to disable the model without deleting the file Model ¶ Field Description LLM Model string Model identifier in provider/model-name format API Base URL Required for Ollama, a gateway such as a LiteLLM proxy, or self-hosted deployments API Key Provider API key; use ${ENV_VAR} syntax to avoid hardcoding secrets Parameters ¶ Field Description Temperature Sampling temperature (0 = deterministic, 2 = creative). Default: 0.7 Max Tokens Maximum completion length. Leave blank to use the provider default Timeout Completion timeout in seconds. Default: 60 AgentModel YAML format ¶ kind: AgentModel version: v1 enabled: true metadata: name: default description: Local Llama 3 via Ollama spec: model: ollama/llama3 api_base: http://localhost:11434 temperature: 0.7 timeout: 60 Provider examples ¶ Ollama (local) spec: model: ollama/llama3 api_base: http://localhost:11434 Run Ollama locally: ollama serve then ollama pull llama3 . OpenAI spec: model: openai/gpt-4o api_key: "${OPENAI_API_KEY}" Anthropic spec: model: anthropic/claude-3-5-sonnet-20241022 api_key: "${ANTHROPIC_API_KEY}" LiteLLM proxy spec: model: litellm_proxy/my-model api_base: http://my-litellm-proxy:4000/v1 api_key: "${LITELLM_API_KEY}" Azure OpenAI spec: model: azure/my-deployment api_base: "https://my-org.openai.azure.com" # or set AZURE_OPENAI_ENDPOINT api_key: "${AZURE_OPENAI_API_KEY}" Using an AI model in a workflow ¶ Reference the model by its metadata.name in an llm or loop agent, a judge, or (for decision models) a decide agent: - id: score_cv description: Score a CV engine: llm inputs: { full_name: str, experience_years: int } outputs: { score: int } budget: { timeout: 20s, max_tokens: 800 } llm: model: default # matches AgentModel metadata.name prompt: Score this CV from 0 to 100. routes: { default: END, parse_error: END.failed, timeout: END.failed, budget_exceeded: END.failed, error: END.failed } In the workflow editor, select the agent and open its Prompt (or Loop ) tab: the AI model dropdown lists the presets configured here, marks disabled ones, and offers Other for a provider/model id of your own. The Decision toggle on this page creates type: decision models ( laya , jev or llm ) for the decide engine . For a hosted decision model, set its API base and an ${ENV_VAR} API key there too. Multiple models ¶ You can define as many AgentModel files as you need. A common pattern is: llms/default.yaml — local Ollama model for fast iteration llms/production.yaml — GPT-4o or Claude for production quality llms/judge.yaml — a dedicated model for LLM-as-a-Judge test evaluation Reference them by name in each workflow step.

docs.text: Reference the model by its metadata.name in an llm or loop agent, a judge, or (for decision models) a decide agent: - id: score_cv description: Score a CV engine: llm inputs: { full_name: str, experience_years: int } outputs: { score: int } budget: { timeout: 20s, max_tokens: 800 } llm: model: default # matches AgentModel metadata.name prompt: Score this CV from 0 to 100. routes: { default: END, parse_error: END.failed, timeout: END.failed, budget_exceeded: END.failed, error: END.failed } In the workflow editor, select the agent and open its Prompt (or Loop ) tab: the AI model dropdown lists the presets configured here, marks disabled ones, and offers Other for a provider/model id of your own. The Decision toggle on this page creates type: decision models ( laya , jev or llm ) for the decide engine . For a hosted decision model, set its API base and an ${ENV_VAR} API key there too.
docs.title: Using an AI model in a workflow

docs.text: You can define as many AgentModel files as you need. A common pattern is: llms/default.yaml — local Ollama model for fast iteration llms/production.yaml — GPT-4o or Claude for production quality llms/judge.yaml — a dedicated model for LLM-as-a-Judge test evaluation Reference them by name in each workflow step.
