docs.title: Authentication & Authorization

docs.text: tuvl's auth stack is built on Ed25519-signed JWTs — offline-verifiable bearer tokens whose claims carry the caller's identity, IAM roles and scopes — backed by a small relational IAM (users, roles, scopes) and enforced by one shared guard on every REST entry point. Authentication answers who is calling (a verified sub claim); authorization answers what they may do ( scopes and groups claims checked against per-resource requirements).
docs.title: Authentication & Authorization

docs.text: Overview Token Anatomy The Verification Pipeline Login & Identity Federation Providers The IAM Model Authorization Surfaces One IAM Implementation Dev Mode vs Production Key Management Failure Modes Reading the Code
docs.title: Table of Contents

docs.text: Two planes, one token: Authentication (who). A caller presents a JWT in Authorization: Bearer <token> . The engine verifies its Ed25519 signature against the process key pair ( alg: EdDSA only) and reads the sub claim. No database lookup is needed to verify a token — verification is fully offline. Authorization (what). The token also carries scopes (fine-grained permissions such as candidate:read ) and groups (the caller's IAM role names). Each protected surface declares a required scope and/or group; enforcement is a set-membership check on the verified claims. login (password / OAuth) request │ │ ▼ ▼ IAM tables ──► mint_token ──► JWT ──────► verify signature (EdDSA), issuer, exp (roles → sub/groups/ │ scopes) scopes/iat/exp ▼ revocation list · session end │ ▼ authorize_token (required scope AND group, iam:admin bypasses both) Key properties: Stateless verification. The IAM database is consulted only at mint time. A token is a snapshot of the user's roles and scopes; role changes take effect on the next mint (login or refresh). Revocation is the one stateful exception. Logout and refresh push the token's SHA-256 hash onto a Redis-backed blacklist checked on every REST request, and narrowing a user's access ends their sessions (below). One guard, every transport. verify_bearer_token and authorize_token in tuvl/core/auth/access.py are the single source of truth for the FastAPI dependencies and MCP export.
docs.title: 1. Overview

docs.text: Tokens are minted by mint_token in tuvl/core/auth/token.py : a JWT signed with the process's Ed25519 key ( alg: EdDSA , header kid = the key id). { "iss": "tuvl", "sub": "3f6c…-uuid", // who the token belongs to "groups": ["hr_manager"], // the user's IAM role names "scopes": ["candidate:read"], // the scopes those roles grant "tenant": "acme", // multi-tenant deployments only "iat": 1760000000.123, // issued at (seconds, ms precision) "exp": 1760086400, // expiry (omitted only with TTL 0) "jti": "9f…" // unique token id } Details that matter: Expiry is signed. With ttl_seconds set (default TUVL_TOKEN_TTL_SECONDS , 86400) the token carries exp ; signature verification itself refuses an expired token. Validated before signing. Group and scope names must match ^[\w:.\-/]+$ , and a tenant id the database session allowlist; the same pattern is enforced by require_scope / require_groups when a guard is declared. Readable, not secret. A JWT's claims are base64, not encrypted: anyone holding the token can read them (that's how clients show who is signed in). Keep secrets and personal data out of claims. The public key is published at GET /auth/jwks.json (RFC 8037 OKP/Ed25519), so gateways and other services can verify tokens themselves. Offline verification can't see logouts or ended sessions — ask tuvl ( /auth/me ) when that matters.
docs.title: 2. Token Anatomy

docs.text: Every REST request passes through the dependency chain in tuvl/core/auth/access.py : Authorization header │ ▼ verify_token / verify_bearer_token ├── 401 if no token ├── dev-mode shortcut: dev key → synthetic iam:admin claims (§9) ├── decode_token: signature (EdDSA only), issuer, sub/iat/iss present, exp ├── token_blacklist.is_revoked(token) ← Redis / in-process └── issued before the user's sessions ended? ← iat vs sessions_ended_at │ ▼ get_current_user(claims) → TokenUser(user_id, groups, scopes, tenant_id) (shape-checked) │ ▼ authorize_token(claims, required_scope=…, required_groups=…) decode_token accepts EdDSA only, so an alg: none token or an HMAC token "signed" with the public key is refused. It requires iss , sub and iat ; a missing or wrong claim, a bad signature or an expired token is a 401. Claims are then shape-checked: groups / scopes must be lists of strings and tenant must pass the tenant allowlist. authorize_token is the single scope/group decision point: A missing subject or a malformed claim → TokenUnauthorizedError (401 / UNAUTHENTICATED ). When both a scope and a group are required, the token must satisfy both (AND, not OR). Within required_groups , membership in any one listed group suffices. iam:admin is the superuser bypass — a token carrying the iam:admin scope satisfies every scope and group requirement and returns immediately. Otherwise a missing scope/group → TokenForbiddenError (403 / PERMISSION_DENIED ). require_scope("x:y") and require_groups([...]) are FastAPI dependency factories that wrap authorize_token and translate its errors to HTTPException s. They validate the scope/group names against the safe-character pattern at router-construction time. bind_principal_context is an async dependency layered on get_current_user that writes the verified user_id (and tenant_id , when the token carries a tenant claim) into request-scoped ContextVars, so structlog and OTel spans annotate every record with the caller identity. Tenant binding is how opt-in multi-tenant deployments scope database sessions; single-tenant deployments can ignore it — the ContextVar simply stays unset. Behavior is pinned by tests/core/test_auth_router.py and tests/core/test_iam_rest.py .
docs.title: 3. The Verification Pipeline

docs.text: All identity endpoints live in tuvl/core/auth/router.py under /auth .
docs.title: 4. Login & Identity

docs.text: POST /auth/bootstrap creates the first administrator. It is only available while tuvl_system_iam_users is empty (409 afterwards) and requires no token. It creates a superadmin role carrying iam:admin , assigns it to the new user, and returns a token.
docs.title: Bootstrap

docs.text: POST /auth/token is a standard OAuth2 password-grant form. The username field is the user's email address (a phone number also matches — lookup is email OR phone_number ). bcrypt off the event loop. Hashing and verification run at cost factor 12 (~200–300 ms of pure CPU) and are always dispatched through run_in_threadpool ( aget_password_hash / averify_password in tuvl/core/auth/crypto.py ), so login never stalls the ASGI event loop. Passwords are truncated to bcrypt's 72-byte limit before hashing, matching bcrypt's own semantics. Login-timing equalisation. When the account is missing, inactive, or passwordless, the handler still verifies the submitted password against a throwaway hash ( _DUMMY_PW_HASH ), so response timing cannot be used to enumerate which emails exist. All failure cases return the same generic 401. On success the handler loads the user's roles and the distinct union of their scopes, and mints a token (§6).
docs.title: Password login

docs.text: Endpoint Behavior GET /auth/me Decodes the calling token; returns user_id , groups , scopes . POST /auth/refresh Re-checks the user is active, revokes the old token, mints a fresh one. POST /auth/logout Revokes the current token (204). Ending a user's sessions. Tokens carry their issue time ( iat , ms). When a user's access shrinks — deactivated, password changed, deleted, a role taken away, or a role they hold deleted or stripped of a scope — the IAM service records sessions ended at now for each affected user, and every token issued before that is refused ( 401 Session ended — sign in again. ). The next sign-in mints a token with the current roles. Granting a role or adding scopes ends nothing; it arrives at the next sign-in. Tokens without iat (minted before this existed) count as older than any end. Revocation ( tuvl/core/auth/blacklist.py ) stores the SHA-256 hex digest of the raw token — never the token itself — with a TTL matching the token lifetime, in Redis when a redis datasource is configured, otherwise in an in-process dict. Multi-worker deployments must configure Redis : without it, a token revoked on one worker is still accepted by the others. There is no server-side session table; the token is the session.
docs.title: Session lifecycle

docs.text: External IdPs are declared as YAML files in the project's federation/ directory, loaded by tuvl/core/auth/federation_loader.py : kind: FederationProvider version: v1 metadata: name: google # matches /auth/oauth/google/… enabled: true spec: provider: google # google | github | microsoft | custom client_id: ${GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID} client_secret: ${GOOGLE_CLIENT_SECRET} # Optional: auth_url / token_url / userinfo_url / scope overrides # tenant_id: common # microsoft only # allowed_domains: [example.com] # allowed_users: [octocat] # github only: login handles, case-insensitive # default_role: member ${VAR} references are resolved from the environment at load time ( ${VAR:default} supports defaults); a provider whose variables are unset is skipped with a warning. Built-in URL defaults exist for Google, GitHub, and Microsoft. A legacy fallback reads TUVL_OAUTH_<PROVIDER>_CLIENT_ID / _CLIENT_SECRET settings when no YAML exists for a built-in provider. The flow is OAuth 2.0 authorization-code: GET /auth/oauth/{provider}/start — stores a one-time state , redirects to the IdP. GET /auth/oauth/{provider}/callback — consumes the state, exchanges the code, fetches the user profile, and upserts an IAM user keyed by (federated_provider, federated_sub) . Account-linking rules in the callback: email_verified is required for auto-link. If an account with the same email already exists but the IdP did not assert the email as verified, the callback returns 403 instead of linking — otherwise an attacker registering an unverified IdP identity under a victim's email could take over the account. For GitHub, only addresses from the verified /user/emails list are trusted. allowed_domains , when set, rejects any email outside the list (403). allowed_users (GitHub) rejects any login handle outside the list (403). New federated users are created passwordless; default_role , when set and existing in the IAM database, is auto-assigned so first-time users don't arrive with zero permissions. The callback returns the same kind of token as password login, or redirects to TUVL_OAUTH_UI_REDIRECT_URL with the token in the URL fragment ( #token=… , so it never reaches a server log) when configured. TUVL_OAUTH_BASE_URL sets the redirect-URI origin registered with the IdP. Device flow (GitHub). A CLI or other headless client signs in without a browser callback: POST /auth/oauth/github/device/start returns handle , user_code , verification_uri , interval , expires_in . GitHub's device code stays on the server. The user opens the URI and enters the code. The client polls POST /auth/oauth/github/device/poll {"handle": …} every interval seconds: 428 while pending, 200 with a token once approved (same account-linking rules as above), 400 when denied or expired. A handle is single-use. Tick Enable Device Flow on the GitHub OAuth app. tuvl register project and Insight's Register dialog use this flow ( project ). Provider YAMLs can be managed at runtime via /auth/admin/federation (list/get/put/delete, iam:admin required); client_secret is redacted in read responses.
docs.title: 5. Federation Providers

docs.text: Four tables, defined in tuvl/core/auth/models.py . All primary keys are UUIDs, safe to embed in tokens. tuvl_system_iam_users tuvl_system_iam_roles ┌──────────────────────────┐ ┌──────────────────────┐ │ id (uuid, pk) │ │ id (uuid, pk) │ │ email (unique) │ │ name (unique) │ │ phone_number (unique) │ │ description │ │ hashed_password (null- │ └─────────┬────────────┘ │ able → federated-only) │ │ │ is_active │ │ │ federated_provider/_sub │ │ └────────────┬─────────────┘ │ │ │ │ tuvl_system_iam_user_roles │ tuvl_system_iam_role_scopes │ ┌───────────────────────┐ │ ┌────────────────────────┐ └──►│ user_id (pk, fk) │ └──►│ role_id (fk, cascade) │ │ role_id (pk, fk) │ │ scope_name │ └───────────────────────┘ └────────────────────────┘ A user authenticates with a bcrypt hashed_password , a federated identity, or both. email is the canonical identity across both paths. A role is a named bundle of scope strings (e.g. hr_manager → requisition:write , candidate:read ). Role names become the token's groups claim. At mint time, the engine collects the user's roles and the distinct union of all their scopes; both are embedded in the token. Deleting a role cascades its scope rows. Users and roles are administered under /auth/admin/users and /auth/admin/roles (full CRUD plus role assignment/revocation), all guarded by iam:admin . Role scope sets are replaced atomically via PATCH /auth/admin/roles/{id}/scopes .
docs.title: 6. The IAM Model

docs.text: Surface Route(s) Requirement Model CRUD /models/{model}/… Off unless the model opts in per operation with spec.api.crud: [list, read, create, update, delete] . Then {model.lower()}:read / :write / :delete by convention; overridable per model via spec.access.{read,write,delete}_scope , optionally pinned to IAM groups via spec.access.{read,write,delete}_groups ; absent entirely when spec.api.expose_model_crud: false Workflow triggers spec.trigger.http.path , and POST /api/workflows/{name}/runs metadata.required_scope and/or metadata.required_group ; a valid bearer token is required even when both are omitted, unless the workflow opts into spec.trigger.http.public: true MCP export /mcp mcp:connect , plus each exported workflow's own trigger gates ( tools/list hides what the caller can't run) Runs GET /api/runs* signed in: your own runs (whoever started a run may follow it); iam:admin reads all Run control POST /api/runs/{id}/pause\|resume\|abort\|steer runs:control Approvals GET /api/approvals , POST /api/approvals/{id} , POST /api/runs/{id}/human/{agent} approvals:decide plus the agent's or tool's required_group ; never the triggering principal when a group is required ( engines ) Engine admin /admin/* (scope catalogue, model versions, …) iam:admin IAM admin /auth/admin/* (users, roles, federation) iam:admin Artifact API /api/artifacts artifacts:read to list/read, artifacts:write to upload (a new version row per upload, never in-place) Dev & Insight /dev/* , /insight dev mode only; the dev session key (§9) Notes: CRUD scope derivation happens in tuvl/core/api/crud_router.py : read_scope = spec.access.read_scope or f"{model_name.lower()}:read" , and likewise for write (POST/PATCH) and delete. Every CRUD route also runs bind_principal_context , so all requests are authenticated even for read. CRUD group pinning. spec.access.read_groups / write_groups / delete_groups (a list, or a bare group name) add an IAM-group requirement alongside the scope — both must be satisfied; require_access(scope, groups) in access.py is the dependency factory each CRUD route depends on, wrapping authorize_token . A tier left undeclared cascades from the next-more-privileged tier ( write_groups falls back to read_groups , delete_groups falls back to write_groups ), so pinning only read_groups never leaves mutations open to a wider audience than reads. Declaring no groups at all is scope-only. iam:admin bypasses every scope and group. Workflow gates are metadata-only. Exactly metadata.required_scope and metadata.required_group gate a workflow — nothing inside agents: changes trigger auth. required_group names an IAM role; membership in that single group is required (alongside the scope, when both are declared). iam:admin bypasses both. Trigger default-deny. Every way of starting a run — the workflow's HTTP route, POST /api/workflows/{name}/runs , and MCP export — requires a valid bearer token by default, even for a workflow that declares neither required_scope nor required_group . Anonymous access is an explicit opt-in via spec.trigger.http.public: true ; tuvl lint project rejects public: true combined with a declared scope or group (V019), and a declared scope/group always wins over public at runtime, so a contradictory config fails closed. The decision is one function, run_denial in tuvl/api/auth.py (over WorkflowAuthPolicy , tuvl/core/auth/workflow_policy.py ), shared by the REST and MCP paths so the enforcement sites can't drift. Scope discovery. GET /admin/scopes (itself iam:admin ) returns every enforceable scope grouped by source — crud (per model, honoring overrides), workflows (per required_scope ), and system ( ["iam:admin"] ) — so an admin composing roles doesn't have to grep YAML. The same response's crud_api_enabled field reports whether the CRUD kill switch (below) is currently on. Run visibility. A principal sees and operates only its own runs unless it holds iam:admin ; a run it can't read is a 404, not a 403, so ids don't leak. Artifact uploads are prompt-level trust. A prompt/steering artifact carries instruction-level authority once a workflow references it, so artifacts:write belongs to the same principals who may edit workflows; iam:admin bypasses both artifact scopes. CRUD kill switch. The entire auto-generated /models/* surface can be turned off project-wide with spec.api.expose_model_crud: false in .tuvl/system.yaml ( SystemConfig ), overridable by the TUVL_EXPOSE_MODEL_CRUD env var (env wins over YAML), and editable from the Insight Settings page's API Access section in dev mode. When disabled, build_crud_routers ( tuvl/core/api/crud_router.py ) never mounts the CRUD routers — the routes are absent, not merely scope-denied — leaving only hand-authored Workflow triggers exposed. Takes effect on restart. Example workflow gate: kind: Workflow metadata: name: screen_candidate required_scope: requisition:write required_group: hr_manager
docs.title: 7. Authorization Surfaces

docs.text: The entire IAM surface — bootstrap, login, session lifecycle, user/role CRUD, federation-provider admin — has exactly one implementation: tuvl/core/auth/iam_service.py . It takes a plain DB session and Python inputs and returns plain results or raises a typed IamError ; it has no FastAPI types. tuvl/core/auth/router.py is a thin REST adapter over it, mapping each IamError subclass to an HTTP status ( NotFoundError → 404, ConflictError → 409, AuthenticationError → 401, ValidationError → 400, ParseError → 422, PersistenceError → 500). The security-relevant behavior lives in the service: login timing-equalization ( iam_service.login always performs one bcrypt comparison, even against DUMMY_PW_HASH for a missing/passwordless account), the federation-provider path sanitizer ( iam_service.safe_federation_path ), and threadpool-offloaded bcrypt and file I/O. The Insight UI calls these REST endpoints directly.
docs.title: 8. One IAM Implementation

docs.text: tuvl dev generates a per-session security key of the form XXXX-XXXX-XXXX-XXXX (uppercase letters + digits, ~83 bits of entropy; tuvl/cli/session.py ) and persists it to .tuvl/.dev-session with mode 0600. The CLI exports TUVL_DEV_MODE=true , TUVL_ALLOW_DEV_AUTH=true , and TUVL_DEV_API_KEY=<key> into the engine process. What the dev key does: Gates the dev surfaces. /dev/* (the dev API Insight uses: project files, validate, codegen, specs, dev runs, breakpoints, judges) is mounted only in dev mode and guarded by a pure-ASGI middleware ( tuvl/core/dev/middleware.py ) enforcing an IP allowlist plus the dev key as bearer token. An unset key fails closed — an empty key never authenticates. Breakpoints, step mode and context editing exist only there. Acts as a superuser credential. In dev mode, verify_token accepts the raw dev key — compared with hmac.compare_digest — and map it to synthetic claims for user dev , group dev , scope iam:admin , minted once per process. The same key therefore works for /dev/* , /auth/admin/* , and every scoped route. --auto-login sets TUVL_DEV_AUTO_LOGIN=1 , which makes the Insight index page embed the key in a <meta name="tuvl-dev-key"> tag so the UI skips its security screen. Off by default. Two boot-time refusals in tuvl/core/auth/access.py keep the shortcut out of production: TUVL_DEV_MODE=true with TUVL_ENV=production aborts the process unconditionally, and outside production dev mode still requires the explicit TUVL_ALLOW_DEV_AUTH=true acknowledgement (which tuvl dev sets for you). When no signing key is configured in dev mode, an ephemeral Ed25519 key pair is generated at startup — tokens become invalid on restart, and a warning says so.
docs.title: Dev mode (tuvl dev)

docs.text: Production runs with dev mode off: no dev key, no /dev or Insight execution surfaces, signed tokens only. TUVL_SIGNING_KEY must be set — TuvlKeyManager ( tuvl/core/auth/keys.py ) fails closed with a RuntimeError pointing at tuvl generate key when the variable is missing outside dev mode.
docs.title: Production (tuvl serve app)

docs.text: The engine signs and verifies all tokens with a single Ed25519 key pair, managed by TuvlKeyManager : # Print a fresh key (and the .env line to paste) tuvl generate key # Or write it straight into the project .env (mode 0600); --force to overwrite tuvl generate key --write TUVL_SIGNING_KEY holds the hex-encoded 32-byte Ed25519 private key (64 hex chars), loaded once per process. The derived public key verifies every incoming token; the private key is used only for minting. Keep the key secret and stable: rotating it invalidates every outstanding token (all users re-login). There is no multi-key rollover; rotation is a hard cutover. Because verification is offline, any process holding only the public key can verify tuvl tokens — fetch it from GET /auth/jwks.json (the kid in each token's header names it). Such a verifier can't see logouts or ended sessions.
docs.title: 10. Key Management

docs.title: 12. Reading the Code

docs.text: Authoring with a coding agent ¶ tuvl can drive the coding agent you already have installed (Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI, …) through the whole path from an idea to a packaged project, with tuvl choosing what the agent is given and what is accepted. There are two ways to work, and both stay open: You do tuvl does Open path Point your agent at the project; it uses the skills in .agents/skills and tuvl serve mcp and builds what it likes. Nothing in the way. tuvl lint project , verify spec , ship and CI still decide what is accepted. Driven path (this page) Decide: pick the idea, review the spec, approve it, merge the pull requests. Numbers everything, gives the agent one narrow job at a time on its own branch, checks the result, records it, opens the pull request. The claim is not that the agent is deterministic. Authoring is free; acceptance is deterministic : the same checks ( lint project , lint spec , verify spec , generate code --check , review , the tests) say yes or no, with no model in the loop. The agent's output is only ever a proposal on a branch. The path ¶ tuvl init who you are, which agent, git on `develop` tuvl import idea brief.pdf IDEA-SK-0004: a numbered, immutable copy of the brief (text extracted) …or `--url <page or ticket>`: a snapshot of a web page, Jira issue or GitHub issue tuvl generate spec --idea IDEA-SK-0004 SPEC-SK-0004-01: your agent drafts it on branch spec/SPEC-SK-0004-01 review, edit …in a pull request (draft), by people tuvl approve spec SPEC-SK-0004-01 who approved it, when, a hash of the body tuvl generate tasks SPEC-SK-0004-01 the task list, derived (no model): TASK-SK-0004-01-001 … tuvl generate code --spec SPEC-SK-0004-01 --all models and workflow skeletons deterministically, then your agent builds each task on its own branch, stacked, each a draft pull request tuvl review code the C-rules and ruff on the Python; --agent adds a second opinion tuvl ship the gate again, then the image and/or a runnable archive Everything except the agent's own steps costs no tokens. tuvl dev shows the same path as a tree (ideas → specs → tasks) in a terminal UI, and Insight shows it in the browser and does the same things. In Insight, on the Ideas page: Upload idea takes files, a folder, links or text you write there and runs tuvl import idea on them (the same numbering from your initials, the same hashes and audit entry; with several files the idea is titled from the first, so give it a title). Generate a spec with my agent runs tuvl generate spec --idea with the agent you chose ( tuvl use agent ), shows its output as it goes, and asks for your consent the first time. The draft goes into the project uncommitted, so the Specs page shows it at once, or onto a spec/<id> branch with nothing pushed (then the idea must be committed: tick Commit it to git when you upload). Then approve the spec and derive its tasks from the same page. An idea from a link ¶ tuvl import idea --url <link> (repeatable, and it mixes with files) saves a snapshot of what the link shows now. In Insight, paste the links one per line in the upload dialog. Link What is saved Credentials (environment variables) Any web page The readable text as Markdown ( <main> or <article> if the page has one; no scripts, menus or footers). Text, JSON, CSV and PDF links are kept as they are none: a page behind a login cannot be read, so save it as a PDF and import the file Jira issue ( …/browse/PAY-12 , or a board link with selectedIssue= ) Summary, status, people, labels, components, description, subtasks, linked issues, attachment names (the files are not fetched) and comments Jira Cloud: TUVL_ATLASSIAN_EMAIL and TUVL_ATLASSIAN_TOKEN (an API token). Server / Data Center: TUVL_ATLASSIAN_PAT Confluence page ( …/spaces/X/pages/123/… or viewpage.action?pageId= ) Title, space, last editor and the page body the same Atlassian variables GitHub issue or pull request Title, state, author, labels, body and the comments (not the diff) TUVL_GITHUB_TOKEN (or GITHUB_TOKEN ) for a private repository A snapshot, like any file. The page is stored in source/ and IDEA.yaml records the link, the kind and when it was fetched; Insight shows it above the text. When the ticket changes, import it again as a new idea that --supersedes the old one. Credentials are sent only to their own service. Atlassian credentials go to *.atlassian.net and to the hosts you list in TUVL_ATLASSIAN_HOSTS (comma separated; for a Server / Data Center host), never to another address; GitHub's go to api.github.com . They are not written to the idea, and a secret in a link's query string ( token , key , sig …) is replaced by … in the recorded link. tuvl does not read .env files: export the variables in the shell that runs tuvl or Insight. Internal addresses are refused (localhost, private ranges, a name that resolves to one) and so is plain http , as for webhooks. For your own Jira or wiki, pass --allow-private (the checkbox in Insight). Redirects are followed by hand and checked at each step; a page may be at most --max-size MB (10). It is sent to your agent like any other file. A ticket can be confidential: the consent you give before generate spec covers it. The prompt marks each snapshot with where it came from and says that text other people can edit is material to specify, not instructions: an agent must not act on a line in a ticket or page that tells it to do something else. Still read the draft spec before you approve it. tuvl import idea --url … --dry-run fetches nothing and lists what would be imported. Ids ¶ IDEA-SK-0004 → SPEC-SK-0004-01 → TASK-SK-0004-01-003 : a spec and a task carry their idea's number, so only the idea id is allocated freely, from your initials (asked by tuvl init ). If two people pick the same number on different branches, tuvl check system finds it and tuvl renumber idea fixes it and every link. What is committed ¶ Committed: idea/ , specs/ (the spec with its approval fields, and its task list), the models, workflows, agents and tests tuvl and your agent write. Not committed (your machine only, git-ignored): .tuvl/agent.yaml (your initials, your agent, your consent), .tuvl/audit/ (the ledger), .tuvl/trace/ (prompts and agent output, by hash), .tuvl/live/ , .tuvl/worktrees/ . What an agent may do ¶ tuvl lets an agent change files only when its headless mode can confine the change; otherwise it is used to review (read and answer) only. Agent Drafts specs and builds tasks Reviews How it is confined Claude Code yes yes --restricted : no code-running tools, file tools limited to the folder, nothing may prompt; review has only Read, Glob, Grep Codex CLI yes yes its sandbox: workspace-write (the folder only), read-only for review Gemini CLI yes yes auto_edit approves edit tools only (a shell call is denied when nothing can answer it); plan for review Antigravity CLI yes yes --mode accept-edits approves edits inside the working folder only; a shell command or an edit outside it is denied. Never --dangerously-skip-permissions . Checked on agy 1.4.10 Cursor, Copilot CLI, Amp no yes no per-run way to allow writes in one folder, so tuvl never grants one generic ( tuvl use agent generic --command '…' ) yes yes not confined: any command that reads the prompt on stdin; only the check of what changed protects you Qwen Code, Aider, OpenCode, Goose not yet not yet listed and detected; headless flags not checked The Claude Code adapter was exercised against the real tool. The others were written from each vendor's documentation and tested with stand-ins; tuvl check agent runs yours once so you can see that it works. Whatever the agent is, tuvl then enforces what it cannot be trusted with: - Scope. generate spec may change one spec file; a codegen task may change its workflow, agents/*.py and artifacts/ . Any other change is reverted and the agent is told which file it may not touch. - Lifecycle fields. id , ideas , status are put back after the agent runs; an approval it writes is removed. An agent cannot approve its own draft, and tuvl never approves for you. - Acceptance. A draft must pass lint spec ; a task must leave its step implemented, with lint project and verify spec agreeing, and the Python without C-rule errors. Findings go back to the agent for another try (3 by default). A task that never passes leaves no branch behind. - Pull requests are opened, never merged. Drafts by default; the stack is based branch on branch. - Consent. Your first agent run asks (or needs --consent ) before idea and project files are sent to your agent; it is recorded in the ledger. - Prompts are not in git. The ledger holds ids, hashes and short details; the full prompt of every run is in .tuvl/trace/ by hash, so you can see exactly what was sent. Review ¶ tuvl review code checks the Python of code agents with rules C001–C012 and ruff , free. Errors fail; --strict makes warnings fail. tuvl review code --agent asks an agent that cannot change anything for a second opinion as JSON findings; it is advisory unless you pass --blocking high . generate code --spec reviews every task before committing it ( --review static by default). Building the UI ¶ ui/specs/ (created by tuvl init ) holds the guidelines for whoever builds the frontend, developer or coding agent. tuvl generate ui-spec writes it from the implemented project, with no model: an index that recommends @tuvl/client (install, generating types, sign-in, the rules for a UI), one file per workflow whose tasks are done (the endpoint and who may call it, the request, every end's status and body, the 202 run lifecycle, the approval form of human steps, real examples from the acceptance cases, a client.execute(...) snippet and a checklist), one for the models with CRUD routes, and ui-contract.json with the same facts as data. generate code --spec adds a workflow's file in the commit of the task that completes it, so what is documented is what exists. Write your own notes below the marker at the end of a file; they survive regeneration. tuvl verify ui-spec fails when the files are stale (use it in CI). Shipping ¶ tuvl ship re-runs the gate first: specs under approval approved and unchanged, lint spec and verify spec clean, tasks done, generated files current, no C-rule errors, a current uv.lock , a clean tree. Then --format image (the default) builds the image labelled with a hash of its runtime files and the commit, --format archive writes a reproducible tar.gz or zip you run with uv on a host without Docker, and both does both. Nothing is deployed; tuvl deploy is for hosted tuvl. CI ¶ tuvl init --ci github (or gitlab ) writes the same gate as CI: on pull requests the checks that fail on errors (a scaffold or a half-built stack legitimately has pending steps), on pushes to develop and main everything --strict . When something stops ¶ You see Because Do No coding agent selected .tuvl/agent.yaml says none tuvl use agent claude X can review code through tuvl, but cannot draft or build yet that agent has no confined write mode pick Claude Code, Codex or Gemini for this step IDEA-… is not committed on develop a draft starts from the base branch tuvl import idea --commit , or commit idea/ is not on develop: merge the spec's pull request first codegen starts from the approved spec merge the spec's PR, or --base spec/SPEC-… is not approved a spec edited after approval is a draft again tuvl approve spec Needs your consent first agent run, no terminal to ask add --consent once the gate failed at ship one of the checks above each line says which, and what to run

docs.text: CLI reference (every command and option) ¶ This page is generated from the command line itself ( python scripts/gen_cli_reference.py ), so it lists every command and every option that exists. CLI reference says what each command is for. -d/--project-dir defaults to the current directory on every command that works on a project. -u/--url ( TUVL_URL ) and -t/--token ( TUVL_TOKEN ) are how the commands that talk to a running server find it. Options written --x/--no-x are on/off switches; the one shown in Default is on unless you switch it. Commands marked toolchain need the developer toolchain ( uv tool install "tuvl[standard]" ). Commands without a verb ¶ tuvl init (toolchain) ¶ Scaffold a new tuvl project: its folders, a database connection, AI model presets and the coding-agent rules and skills; --sample adds a working example. Arguments: [name] Option Value Default What it does --project-dir , -d DIRECTORY Alias for the NAME argument — path to scaffold the project into. --sample A 2.0 sample: ticket triage with a spec, task plan, tests and lock that pass the CI gate. --multi-tenant Enable multi-tenancy. Requires a PostgreSQL datasource to be configured at init time. The mode is locked into the database on first boot and cannot be changed without re-initialising. --no-ai-skills Skip scaffolding the .agents/ directory containing AI agent rules and skills. --preset TEXT LLM preset: gemini, openai, anthropic or ollama (current model ids; the key is read from the environment, else left blank in .env). --yes , -y Accept every default without prompting (CI, coding agents). --decision-model TEXT Decision model for decide agents: laya (a self-hosted laya-serve container, added to tuvl ship ) or none. --agent TEXT Coding agent tuvl may run for you (see --list-agents), or none . Asked when omitted. --no-agent Same as --agent none. --list-agents Show the coding agents found on this machine and exit. --initials TEXT Your initials (2-4 letters/digits); they stamp the ids of ideas and specs you create. --git/--no-git on Run git init on the project when git is installed. --branch TEXT develop The initial git branch. --commit Make an initial commit. --ci TEXT none Write the deterministic gate as CI: github (.github/workflows/tuvl.yml), gitlab (.gitlab-ci.yml) or none. --dev-telemetry TEXT https address of your team's telemetry collector (optional; tuvl set dev-telemetry changes it later). tuvl dev (toolchain) ¶ Run the engine in development mode: hot reload, the Insight editor at /insight and the terminal UI. Option Value Default What it does --port , -p INTEGER 8885 Port to bind the engine on. --project-dir , -d DIRECTORY Path to the tuvl project directory (contains models/, workflows/, etc.). Defaults to current directory. --no-browser Skip opening the UI in a browser. --allow-host , -H TEXT (repeatable) Allow remote connections from this IP or CIDR (e.g. --allow-host 192.168.1.0/24). Can be repeated. Localhost is always permitted. --show-key Print the generated dev API key to the terminal. Off by default so the key is not captured by shell history, recording tools, or shared screens. The key is always persisted to /.tuvl/.dev-session (mode 0600). --auto-login Automatically bypass the security screen in Tuvl Insight. --no-tui Run the engine in this terminal as before, without the terminal UI that starts on a terminal. tuvl ship (toolchain) ¶ Package the project for production — validate, containerize, and emit a Helm chart. Option Value Default What it does --project-dir , -d DIRECTORY . Path to the tuvl project directory (contains config.yaml, models/, workflows/, etc.). --tag , -t TEXT Image reference to build. Defaults to : . --no-build , --no-image Write the Dockerfile and Helm chart but skip the docker build. --format TEXT image image (a docker image and a Helm chart), archive (the runtime files as a project you run with uv) or both. --archive-format TEXT tar.gz tar.gz or zip. --out PATH dist Where the archive is written. --allow-incomplete Ship although some spec tasks are not done. --allow-dirty Ship although the working tree has uncommitted changes. --push Push the image after a successful build. --force Overwrite existing generated files (deploy/, .dockerignore). --strict Treat validation warnings as errors. --extra TEXT (repeatable) Also install this tuvl extra (mcp, redis, vector) — for a feature the project turns on in a way tuvl ship cannot see. Repeatable. --with-laya/--without-laya Add a Laya decision server (laya-serve) to the Helm chart. Default: on when an AgentModel uses provider: laya. tuvl deploy (toolchain) ¶ Deploy to managed tuvl hosting (coming soon: prints a message and exits 1). Option Value Default What it does --project-dir , -d PATH . Path to the tuvl project (not used yet). tuvl create ¶ tuvl create spec ¶ Write specs/ .md from the template (numbered and linked to its idea with --idea). Arguments: <name> Option Value Default What it does --project-dir , -d PATH . tuvl project directory --owner TEXT Owning team --workflow TEXT Workflow the examples run (default: from name) --idea TEXT (repeatable) The idea(s) it comes from; numbers the spec SPEC-XX-NNNN-NN tuvl import ¶ tuvl import idea ¶ Copy an idea (files, a folder, or a snapshot of a URL) into idea/IDEA- -NNNN/ as a numbered, immutable record. Arguments: [paths] Option Value Default What it does --project-dir , -d PATH . tuvl project directory --url TEXT (repeatable) A web page, Jira issue, Confluence page or GitHub issue to snapshot (repeatable) --allow-private Let --url reach internal addresses (your own Jira or wiki) --title TEXT Idea title (default: first heading) --supersedes TEXT The idea this one replaces (IDEA-XX-NNNN) --initials TEXT Your initials (saved on first use) --include TEXT (repeatable) Only these globs --exclude TEXT (repeatable) Skip these globs --max-size INTEGER 10 Largest file, in MB --dry-run Show what would be imported --commit Commit the new idea (needed before generate spec can use it) --json Machine-readable result tuvl use ¶ tuvl use agent ¶ Choose the coding agent tuvl may run for you, or none . Stored in .tuvl/agent.yaml . Arguments: <agent> Option Value Default What it does --project-dir , -d PATH . tuvl project directory --force Select an agent that was not found on this machine --command TEXT For generic : the command to run. It reads the prompt on stdin and edits the working directory, e.g. --command 'mytool --yes'. tuvl set ¶ tuvl set dev-telemetry ¶ Turn developer telemetry on, off or change it. Commit the file; your token stays in your own config folder. Arguments: [server] Option Value Default What it does --off Stop sending (the settings stay) --identity TEXT What the events say about you: initials (default) or full (name and email) --token-env TEXT Environment variable that overrides your registered token (default TUVL_DEV_TELEMETRY_TOKEN) --commands/--no-commands Also send one event per command run --forget Delete your registered token for this collector from this machine --rotate-token Get a new token from the collector; the old one stops working --project-dir , -d PATH . tuvl project directory tuvl set project ¶ Update one field. The description is Markdown. Arguments: <field> <value> Option Value Default What it does --project-dir , -d DIRECTORY . Project directory. tuvl upgrade ¶ tuvl upgrade project ¶ Create project.yaml for a project that predates it. Never changes an existing id. Option Value Default What it does --project-dir , -d DIRECTORY . Project directory. --name TEXT Defaults to the directory name. --new-id Replace the id (copied project) and clear its registration. tuvl register ¶ tuvl register developer ¶ Register yourself at the team's collector and keep your token (it sends and reads for you). Option Value Default What it does --name TEXT Your name (default: your git name) --email TEXT Your email (default: your git email) --code TEXT The team's join code, from whoever runs the collector --project-dir , -d PATH . tuvl project directory tuvl register project ¶ List this project in the public catalogue (shows the payload first). Project directory. --nest TEXT Registry URL (TUVL_NEST_URL). --yes , -y Skip the confirmation. tuvl update ¶ tuvl update skills ¶ Refresh AGENTS.md and the skills to this tuvl version (removes the 1.x skills). docs.text: This page is generated from the command line itself ( python scripts/gen_cli_reference.py ), so it lists every command and every option that exists. CLI reference says what each command is for. -d/--project-dir defaults to the current directory on every command that works on a project. -u/--url ( TUVL_URL ) and -t/--token ( TUVL_TOKEN ) are how the commands that talk to a running server find it. Options written --x/--no-x are on/off switches; the one shown in Default is on unless you switch it. Commands marked toolchain need the developer toolchain ( uv tool install "tuvl[standard]" ).

docs.text: Scaffold a new tuvl project: its folders, a database connection, AI model presets and the coding-agent rules and skills; --sample adds a working example. Arguments: [name] Option Value Default What it does --project-dir , -d DIRECTORY Alias for the NAME argument — path to scaffold the project into. --sample A 2.0 sample: ticket triage with a spec, task plan, tests and lock that pass the CI gate. --multi-tenant Enable multi-tenancy. Requires a PostgreSQL datasource to be configured at init time. The mode is locked into the database on first boot and cannot be changed without re-initialising. --no-ai-skills Skip scaffolding the .agents/ directory containing AI agent rules and skills. --preset TEXT LLM preset: gemini, openai, anthropic or ollama (current model ids; the key is read from the environment, else left blank in .env). --yes , -y Accept every default without prompting (CI, coding agents). --decision-model TEXT Decision model for decide agents: laya (a self-hosted laya-serve container, added to tuvl ship ) or none. --agent TEXT Coding agent tuvl may run for you (see --list-agents), or none . Asked when omitted. --no-agent Same as --agent none. --list-agents Show the coding agents found on this machine and exit. --initials TEXT Your initials (2-4 letters/digits); they stamp the ids of ideas and specs you create. --git/--no-git on Run git init on the project when git is installed. --branch TEXT develop The initial git branch. --commit Make an initial commit. --ci TEXT none Write the deterministic gate as CI: github (.github/workflows/tuvl.yml), gitlab (.gitlab-ci.yml) or none. --dev-telemetry TEXT https address of your team's telemetry collector (optional; tuvl set dev-telemetry changes it later).

docs.text: Run the engine in development mode: hot reload, the Insight editor at /insight and the terminal UI. Option Value Default What it does --port , -p INTEGER 8885 Port to bind the engine on. --project-dir , -d DIRECTORY Path to the tuvl project directory (contains models/, workflows/, etc.). Defaults to current directory. --no-browser Skip opening the UI in a browser. --allow-host , -H TEXT (repeatable) Allow remote connections from this IP or CIDR (e.g. --allow-host 192.168.1.0/24). Can be repeated. Localhost is always permitted. --show-key Print the generated dev API key to the terminal. Off by default so the key is not captured by shell history, recording tools, or shared screens. The key is always persisted to /.tuvl/.dev-session (mode 0600). --auto-login Automatically bypass the security screen in Tuvl Insight. --no-tui Run the engine in this terminal as before, without the terminal UI that starts on a terminal.

docs.text: CLI reference ¶ Commands are actions: tuvl <verb> <thing> . Every command that reports supports --json with a stable, documented schema (coding agents parse it; /dev/schema/cli serves the schemas in dev mode). -d/--project-dir defaults to the current directory everywhere. Every option of every command, with its value and default, is on the generated full option reference . The verbs ¶ Each verb makes one kind of promise, so the name tells you what a command will do. Verb Promise Things generate Writes files. Spends tokens only where a coding agent is involved spec , tasks , code , ui-spec , lock , key , rls lint Static rules over what you wrote. Offline, zero tokens project , spec verify Is one thing still in step with another? Exits 1 on drift spec , lock , ui-spec , rls , audit check Is it reachable and working right now? Touches the live environment system , agent , storage review A judgement of code code approve / reject / reopen A human decision, recorded in the audit ledger spec create / import / renumber Make or bring in specs and ideas spec / idea / idea list / show Only read ideas , specs , tasks , runs , agents , objects / idea , run , event , audit , drift , project run Run a workflow or the tests workflow , tests serve Start a server app , mcp follow / pin / replay Work with runs run / run / runs use / set / upgrade / register / update Project setup agent / project / project / project / skills export / prune Admin audit , schema / traces , memory init , dev , ship , deploy One action each Project ¶ Command Options tuvl init [NAME] --dev-telemetry URL , --sample , --preset gemini\|openai\|anthropic\|ollama , --decision-model laya\|none , -y/--yes , --multi-tenant , --no-ai-skills , --agent , --no-agent , --list-agents , --initials , --git/--no-git , --branch , --commit , --ci github\|gitlab\|none Scaffold a project. A preset writes llms/default.yaml with a current model id, reading the key from the environment. --sample is a ticket-triage project (spec, TaskPlan, tests, lock) that passes the CI gate as created. --decision-model laya adds llms/laya.yaml , LAYA_API_* in .env and a compose.yaml that runs laya-serve locally (asked interactively, default no). -y accepts every default. It also asks for your initials (they stamp the ids of ideas and specs you create) and, when coding agents are installed, which one tuvl may run for you ( -y picks none), writes both to .tuvl/agent.yaml (git-ignored), and runs git init on branch develop when git is installed ( --ci github or gitlab also writes the deterministic gate as CI: errors fail on pull requests, everything --strict on pushes to develop / main ) and the project is not already inside a repository ( --commit makes an initial commit) tuvl list agents / use agent <agent\|none> / check agent -d , --json (list), --force , --command (use) The coding agents on this machine (Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI, Antigravity, Cursor, Copilot CLI, Amp, Qwen Code, Aider, OpenCode, Goose), the one you selected, and whether tuvl can run it: yes for an agent tuvl can let draft and build (Claude Code, Codex CLI, Gemini CLI, Antigravity CLI: their headless modes can confine a write to the folder), review only for one it can ask to review but never to write (Cursor, Copilot CLI, Amp), detected, not yet for the rest. The choice is yours alone, in .tuvl/agent.yaml (git-ignored). check agent checks the selected agent starts, then runs it once on a trivial task in a scratch folder (a few tokens; -y skips the question). use generic --command '…' selects any command that reads a prompt on stdin and edits its working directory tuvl check storage [name] / list objects <name> [prefix] --json (check); -n/--limit (list, default 100) Check each kind: Storage store by writing, reading back and deleting a probe object (read-only stores are only listed), or list a store's objects. See docs/storage.md tuvl lint project --strict , --json Contracts, data flow, types, policy, artifacts, lock; prints each workflow's determinism profile and worst-case tokens. --strict fails on warnings. Ends with needs models : every model the workflows use, its provider and the environment variables it reads (or "no LLM required"); V028 = unknown model reference, V029 = undeclared credentials (an error at ship time) tuvl generate code [WORKFLOW] --check Schemas, code-agent stubs (body-preserving merge), prompt placeholders, spec tests. --check writes nothing and exits 1 on drift tuvl generate code --spec SPEC --task 3 \| --task 1,3 \| --all --no-agent , --agent , --max-attempts 3 , --budget USD , --timeout S , --model , --base , --no-pr , --ready , --continue , --keep-worktree , --consent , --review none\|static\|agent , --review-blocking , --reviewer Build an approved spec's models and workflows from its task list. Phase 1, deterministic, zero tokens: the missing models/*.yaml from # Data , a workflows/<flow>.yaml skeleton whose steps are all pending (trigger, ends, and every step's id, inputs, outputs, routes and budget come from # Flows ), then the generated schemas, stubs, prompt placeholders and tests; one branch feature/<SPEC>-scaffold , never overwriting an existing file. Phase 2, your coding agent, one task at a time: for each selected agent task a branch feature/TASK-… stacked on the one before, in a worktree; the agent replaces that one pending step and may touch only the workflow, agents/*.py and artifacts/ ; tuvl regenerates what is generated and accepts the task only when the step is implemented and lint project and verify spec agree (findings go back to the agent), then commits and, with a remote and gh / glab , pushes and opens a draft pull request based on the previous branch. Before a task is committed its Python is reviewed ( --review static , the default: the C-rules and ruff, errors fail the task and go back to the agent; agent adds a second opinion that lands in the pull request and blocks only with --review-blocking ). Failed tasks leave no branch and stop the run ( --continue goes on with independent ones). Re-running skips what is built. Task numbers: 3 , T3 , 003 or the full id. --no-agent stops after phase 1. Without --spec , tuvl generate code never calls an agent tuvl generate ui-spec / verify ui-spec -w/--workflow , --all , --no-tests , --base-url , --check , --json , -d ( verify ui-spec takes --no-tests , --base-url , --json : exit 1 when ui/specs/ is not what generate would write now) Write ui/specs/ (zero tokens): how to build the UI on this backend , for the developers and coding agents who build it. README.md (the @tuvl/client setup, sign-in, the backend surface: which system routes a production server mounts, shared behaviour, rules for whoever builds the UI), one <workflow>.md per workflow whose tasks are done (endpoint, auth, request, every end's status and body, the run lifecycle, the approval form of human steps, real examples from the acceptance cases, a client.execute(...) snippet, a checklist), models.md for models with CRUD routes (operations, scopes, groups, fields, secure flagged), and ui-contract.json . init creates the folder; codegen --spec adds a workflow's file in the commit of the task that completes it. Text below the notes marker in a file is kept. --check exits 1 when a file is missing or out of date (add it to CI); a workflow with a pending step or open task gets no file until it is built ( --all writes it anyway) tuvl review code [PATH…] --base REF , --spec SPEC , --task 3 , --strict , --no-ruff , --explain C0xx , --json ; second opinion: --agent , --reviewer , --blocking off\|high\|medium\|low , --post , --consent , --budget , --timeout Review the Python of code agents ( agents/*.py , not _generated ); --spec or --task keeps it to the code agents those tasks created (models, steps that are not code, tests and examples have none). Tier 1, free: tuvl's rules — C001 shape ( @agent("run") async def f(inp, ctx) ), C002 processes and eval , C003 direct network (use ctx.http ), C004 os.environ , C005 file writes (use ctx.storage ), C006 non-determinism (random, uuid, clock), C007/C008 work or state kept in the module, C009 hard-coded URLs, C010 secrets, C011 a returned signal the workflow does not route, C012 a write in an effect: read agent — plus ruff (C900) when installed. Errors fail (exit 1), warnings only with --strict . Tier 2, advisory: --agent asks a coding agent that cannot change anything (Claude Code runs with only Read, Glob and Grep) to read the code, the diff and the spec and answer with JSON findings (high / medium / low / info); an answer that is not valid JSON is a failed review, never a pass. Findings only block with --blocking . --post comments the review on the branch's pull request. The reviewer is another agent than yours when you have one tuvl generate lock / verify lock --check , --mcp/--no-mcp Pin model ids, artifact hashes, judge/decision models and MCP tool schemas in tuvl.lock ; verify lock is the read-only check (exit 1 when the lock is missing or stale; --no-mcp skips listing MCP servers live) tuvl check system --live , --json , --only , --skip , --strict , --fix , -q , --verbose Is the project healthy? Runs named check groups, each check ok / warn / fail / skip: project (identity record), env (Python range, .env present and git-ignored, uv ), config (the project loads), models (each model, the variables it needs and which are missing; --live makes one minimal call per model — Laya/Jev: their /health ), storage , and, where the toolchain is installed, git (repository, branch, identity, remote) and skills ( AGENTS.md , .agents/skills ). --only / --skip take comma-separated group names. Exit 1 on any failure; --strict exits 2 when only warnings remain. --fix applies the safe repairs a check offers ( git init -b develop , adding .env to .gitignore ) and re-checks; nothing destructive. A production server runs the model check at startup and refuses to start on a missing variable; /health reports each model's readiness tuvl run tests --live , --allow-uncertain , --strict , -k/--only TEXT , --json Run Test documents offline ( --live lets unmocked model/tool agents call out). Results are PASS, STUBBED (expectations met only through unmocked pending placeholders — not counted) or FAIL; --strict (CI) also fails on stubbed results and untrusted judge calibration tuvl show project --json The project's identity from .tuvl/project.yaml : the immutable, self-checking id ( prj_<uuidv7>-<2 check characters> , minted by tuvl init ; the check catches typos and hand edits, it is not a signature), name, author, email, type ( poc\|dev\|production ), version, registry status. Also editable in Insight → Settings → Project. Full reference: project tuvl upgrade project --name , --new-id Create project.yaml for a project that predates it. Never changes an existing id; --new-id replaces a malformed or copied id and clears its registration tuvl set dev-telemetry [URL] --off , --identity initials\|full , --token-env VAR , --commands/--no-commands , --forget , --rotate-token Share developer actions through your team's collector (optional, off by default; tuvl init can ask for it). Writes .tuvl/dev-telemetry.yaml (commit it); your token is never in it. --forget removes your token from this machine. See developer telemetry tuvl register developer --name , --email , --code Register yourself at the team's collector with its join code and keep the token of your own in your config folder; it sends your events and reads the team's tuvl show dev-telemetry / check dev-telemetry --json / --flush Whether it is on, who you are at the collector, what is queued and the last delivery; ask the collector who your token is (exit 1 when it does not accept it) and, with --flush , send everything queued tuvl list team-activity --actor , --entity , --kind , -n , --json What the team did on this project, from the collector tuvl set project FIELD VALUE Update name , author , email , type , version , description , license or repo (validated). The description is Markdown (up to 2000 characters): VALUE of @about.md reads a file, - reads stdin; show project renders it tuvl register project --nest URL , -y List the project in the public catalogue. Prints the exact payload first and asks; signs in with GitHub's device flow; the author and email are sent for contact and never shown publicly. Also available as Insight → Settings → Project → Register / Update listing (same payload preview and login) tuvl update skills --diff Refresh AGENTS.md and .agents/skills/ to this tuvl version (removes 1.x skills; mirrors to .claude/skills/ ) Specs ¶ Command Options tuvl verify spec [SPEC_FILE…] --strict , --no-tests , --json Does the implementation match the spec? Zero tokens; rules R001–R010 and a traceability matrix (step → agent → tests). Exits 1 on a mismatch ( --strict : also on unfinished work) tuvl create spec NAME --owner , --workflow Write specs/<name>.md from the template tuvl import idea [PATH…] --url (repeatable), --allow-private , --title , --supersedes , --initials , --include , --exclude , --max-size , --commit , --dry-run , --json Copy an idea (files, a folder, or a snapshot of a web page, Jira issue, Confluence page or GitHub issue given with --url ; see authoring ) into idea/IDEA-<INITIALS>-NNNN/source/ as a numbered, immutable record, with IDEA.yaml (file hashes, who, when) and idea/INDEX.yaml . Text is extracted from Markdown/text directly, from Word files with no extra install, and from PDFs with tuvl[pdf] (a scanned PDF has no text layer and gets a warning; there is no OCR) into extracted/ . Secret and key files, hidden files, symbolic links and unsupported types are skipped and listed. Ids are IDEA-SK-0004 → SPEC-SK-0004-01 → TASK-SK-0004-01-003 : the spec and task ids inherit the idea's number. Initials come from .tuvl/agent.yaml ( --initials saves them on first use) tuvl list ideas / show idea ID --json List the ideas and the specs generated from each / show one idea's files, hashes and specs tuvl list branches [SPEC] --json Where the branches of each spec's work stand: the spec, the scaffold and one per agent task, as a tree of what grew from what (branches built apart from each other sit side by side and are marked parallel), with each branch's commits and messages. Each is merged (on the base branch, even if the branch was deleted), open (built, not merged: commits ahead and behind, last commit, pull request) or not built, with what to merge next. tuvl never merges; it prints the command tuvl show task TASK-ID --spec SPEC , --json One task in full: what it builds, what it waits for and the spec section it came from; after a failed generate code run, also the report of each attempt (the check it failed, the problems, the end of the agent's output), kept until the task succeeds. A legacy T3 needs --spec tuvl renumber idea IDEA --to IDEA-XX-NNNN After two developers picked the same number: give the idea a new one (default the next free) and carry its spec and task ids, file names, links and the task lists' spec hash along. tuvl check system (group ideas ) reports duplicate ids and an idea the base branch already numbers differently tuvl approve spec SPEC / reject spec SPEC --reason … / reopen spec SPEC --force (approve) Approve a spec (by id, name or file): records who, when and a hash of the body in its front matter; refuses while lint spec has errors. Editing the body afterwards makes the approval stale (S017). reject sends it back to draft with a reason; reopen withdraws an approval tuvl generate tasks SPEC --dry-run Derive the task list from an approved spec, with no model: one task per new model, step and example, a manual task for each external-system step. Keeps ids, refreshes section hashes, marks removed ones obsolete ; --dry-run previews a draft tuvl list specs --json Each spec's id, status (draft / approved / approved but changed), approver and ideas tuvl prune memory COLLECTION --key OWNER or --older-than 30d (exactly one), -d Erases what agents remember: every memory of one owner, or all older than an age, in one memory collection. Prints how many rows went and deletes nothing else (knowledge-base rows and other collections are untouched). See Remembering across runs tuvl show audit / show event REF / verify audit / export audit / prune traces --entity , --actor , --kind , --since 2d , -n , --follow , --json (log); --format json\|csv , -o (export); --older-than DAYS (prune) The local audit ledger .tuvl/audit/<YYYY-MM>.jsonl (git-ignored): one hash-chained event per action with side effects — init, agent choice, idea import, id renumber, spec create / approve / reject / reopen (refusals too, with the reason), task derivation. It holds ids, hashes and short details, never file contents, prompts or secrets (full prompts and agent output go to .tuvl/trace/ by hash). --entity on an idea also shows its specs and tasks. verify finds an edited, removed or reordered line (exit 1); prune deletes old trace files, never the ledger. The ledger belongs to one machine and one developer: what the team shares through git is the spec's own approval fields tuvl create spec NAME --idea IDEA-… Also numbers the spec SPEC-XX-NNNN-NN after its first idea, links it to the idea(s) and records status: draft tuvl generate spec --idea IDEA-… \| --from PATH --title , --agent , --max-attempts 3 , --budget USD , --timeout S , --model , --base , --dry-run , --show-prompt , -y , --consent , --no-pr , --ready , --keep-worktree , --here A coding agent writes a draft spec from an idea. tuvl numbers it ( SPEC-XX-NNNN-NN ), creates branch spec/<id> in a worktree under .tuvl/worktrees/ , builds the prompt (the idea's text, the spec grammar, the rules), runs your agent headlessly, lets it change only that spec file (anything else is reverted and fed back), puts back the lifecycle fields it must not set ( id , ideas , status , no approval), runs lint spec and retries with the findings, then commits and, with a remote and gh / glab , pushes and opens a draft pull request. It never merges and never approves. --here skips the branch and the pull request and writes specs/<id>.md into your working folder, uncommitted (the terminal UI uses it, so the draft shows up in the tree). Needs git; the idea must be committed ( spec import --commit ; --from does it). With Claude Code the run is restricted at the source (no code-running tools, files confined to the folder, nothing may prompt); generic ( tuvl use agent generic --command '…' ) cannot be restricted, only checked afterwards. Idea text is sent to your agent only after you consent once ( --consent , stored in .tuvl/agent.yaml ) tuvl lint spec [SPEC_FILE…] --strict , --json Is the spec complete and consistent? Zero tokens; rules S001–S016 with line numbers, plus P001–P005 on its task list ( spec-driven ). Exits 1 on a blocking finding ( --strict : on warnings too) tuvl list tasks [SPEC_FILE] --strict , --no-tests , --json , --watch , --interval Derived task statuses. --strict exits 1 unless every live task is done and none is blocked or stale. --watch keeps refreshing (recomputing only when a project file changes) and overlays live generate code progress (queued, running attempt n/N and its gate, failed, in review) from .tuvl/live/tasks.json tuvl show drift [SPEC_FILE] --json Stale tasks and spec sections no task covers Servers ¶ Command Options tuvl dev -p/--port (8885), --auto-login , --no-tui , --show-key , --no-browser , --no-tui , -H/--allow-host Dev server with Insight and the dev API, reloading on YAML changes. The session key is stored in .tuvl/.dev-session (0600); --show-key prints it. On a terminal it also starts a terminal UI ( tuvl[tui] , part of tuvl[standard] ): a tree of your ideas → specs → tasks (status, and live progress while generate code runs), the actions that apply to what you select (check, approve, derive tasks, scaffold, build with your agent, validate, test, ship…), and three logs: the command you ran, the engine, and the audit trail. Every action runs the same tuvl command you would type, so the gates and the audit trail are the same; anything that spends your agent's tokens or is hard to undo asks first ( Run it / Cancel ) and says so. The project's own actions (lint, test, check, review, run a workflow, import an idea, show the project and the audit log, ship) are listed under every selection. Each command ends with a tokens · line: what your coding agent used (input, output, cost), or that none was. q quits and stops the engine, r refreshes, x stops a running command, c copies the last command's output (or the open log) to the clipboard. The logs are selectable too: drag with the mouse, or click in a log and use the keyboard, then copy with ctrl+c . --no-tui , or no terminal (CI, a pipe, ssh without a tty), runs the engine in this terminal with plain output tuvl serve app -p/--port , --host , -w/--workers , --role all\|api\|worker , -c/--concurrency (8), -H/--allow-host , --graceful-timeout , --drain-timeout , --forwarded-allow-ips , --limit-max-requests Production server (uvicorn, which replaces the tuvl process so it is PID 1 in a container and receives SIGTERM directly). api serves HTTP and runs synchronous requests inline; worker executes the queue. On SIGTERM it stops taking requests, lets open ones finish for --graceful-timeout seconds (20), then waits --drain-timeout seconds (20) for running runs; one still going is interrupted and another worker resumes it from its last checkpoint. --forwarded-allow-ips names the proxies whose X-Forwarded-For is trusted (an IP or CIDR list: set your ingress network so --allow-host and the logs see the real client; * lets a client spoof its address). --limit-max-requests restarts a worker after that many requests. The Server header is off. tuvl run with no subcommand does the same tuvl serve mcp --allow-write Dev tools for coding agents over MCP (stdio); --allow-write adds codegen_write , run_workflow , pin_fixture . Refuses production Runs ¶ These talk to a running server: -u/--url ( TUVL_URL , default http://localhost:8885 ) and -t/--token ( TUVL_TOKEN , needs runs:read ). Command Options tuvl list runs -w/--workflow , -s/--status , -n/--limit , --json Recent runs, newest first tuvl show run RUN_ID One run as JSON tuvl follow run RUN_ID / run workflow NAME -p/--payload JSON (run workflow) Follow a run's events until it ends, or start a run of a workflow on the server and follow it; exits 1 if it fails tuvl pin run RUN_ID -n/--name Export the journal to tests/fixtures/<workflow>/<name>.journal.json tuvl replay runs FIXTURES… --json Re-run pinned journals offline; fail if the end or output differ Shipping and operations ¶ Command Options tuvl ship -t/--tag , --no-image (was --no-build ), --push , --force , --strict , --extra , --with-laya/--without-laya , --format image\|archive\|both , --archive-format tar.gz\|zip , --out , --allow-incomplete , --allow-dirty Gate (validate, no pending agents — V010 is an error at ship time, current lock; then, once the files are written, the deterministic spec gate : every spec under approval is approved and unchanged, lint spec and verify spec have no errors, every task is done ( --allow-incomplete ), generated files are current ( codegen --check , for projects with specs), no C-rule errors in the agents' Python, a current uv.lock (an error for the archive), and a clean git tree ( --allow-dirty ; what ship writes itself does not count). A spec with no status: only warns), then .dockerignore as an allowlist (only models, workflows, agents, artifacts, datasources, llms, federation, config, lock and .tuvl/system.yaml / telemetry.yaml enter the image; specs, task lists, tests, agent rules and skills, compose files and anything else stay out — V027 refuses development files), deploy/Dockerfile (pins the locked tuvl version and installs only the extras the project uses: mcp for use: mcp tools, loop MCP servers and MCP export, redis for a redis datasource, vector for collections and tuvl.data_* , otel-grpc for otlp_protocol: grpc ; it also stops when agents/*.py imports a package pyproject.toml does not declare. --extra NAME adds one the scan cannot see; the choice is recorded as the image label io.tuvl.extras ) and a Helm chart ( split: true for api + worker Deployments; a Laya Deployment + Service, with LAYA_API_BASE set for the engine, when a model uses provider: laya or with --with-laya — laya.enabled in values.yaml) and docker build , labelled io.tuvl.runtime-hash (one sha256 over the runtime files) and io.tuvl.git-commit . --format archive instead writes dist/<name>-<version>.tar.gz (or .zip ) plus a .sha256 : the same runtime files with run.sh , RUN.md , .env.example and BUILD-INFO.json , reproducible byte for byte from the same files, for hosts without Docker. On the host: tar xzf … , cp .env.example .env , fill it in, ./run.sh (needs uv ; it installs the locked dependencies and tuvl==<locked> with the same extras as the image, and serves on port 8885) tuvl deploy -d/--project-dir Coming soon: deploy to a hosted, managed tuvl engine that runs your backend services. Today it prints a message, deploys nothing and exits 1 tuvl generate key -w/--write , -f/--force A persistent Ed25519 key for signing access tokens ( TUVL_SIGNING_KEY ) tuvl generate rls -o/--out Idempotent row-level-security SQL for tenant-scoped tables tuvl verify rls Exit 1 if a tenant-scoped table lacks its RLS policy Extras: what an image installs ¶ tuvl installs lean. Features with their own packages are extras, and tuvl ship reads the project and installs tuvl[<only those>]==<locked version> : Extra Package tuvl ship installs it when mcp mcp a use: mcp tool, a loop mcp tool, or a workflow with trigger.mcp.enabled redis redis a kind: DataSource with type: redis , or agents/*.py imports redis vector pgvector a Collection or Embedding document, tuvl.data_search / tuvl.data_ingest , or an import of pgvector otel-grpc OTLP gRPC exporter .tuvl/telemetry.yaml has otlp_protocol: grpc generate code , run tests libcst , aiosqlite never: tuvl generate code , tuvl init --sample and tuvl run tests are development tools tuvl[standard] installs Insight and every extra, so a development install needs nothing else. The model providers and blob storage (S3, Azure, GCS, local) are part of tuvl and need no extra. tuvl ship prints the extras it chose and why and records them as the image label io.tuvl.extras ( docker inspect shows what an image carries). Beyond the extras: It also scans agents/*.py : an import of a package that pyproject.toml does not declare aborts the ship, because the image would fail at run time. Declared packages that no agent imports are listed and kept. --extra NAME adds an extra the scan cannot see, for example a feature switched on by an environment variable. It accepts mcp , redis , vector and otel-grpc . A kept deploy/Dockerfile (no --force ) that lacks an extra the project now needs stops the ship. Using a feature without its extra fails with pip install 'tuvl[name]' ; the same message appears for tuvl generate code , tuvl run tests and tuvl serve mcp on a bare install. tuvl deploy is for managed hosting and is not available yet: it prints a message and exits 1. Until then, install the chart tuvl ship writes with helm . The CI gate ¶ tuvl lint spec && tuvl lint project --strict && tuvl generate code --check && tuvl verify lock && tuvl run tests --strict && tuvl verify spec --strict && tuvl list tasks --strict
